name: Peter
sum: The fisherman Jesus called the Rock, chief of the Apostles and first Bishop of Rome.
bio: Simon was a fisherman from Bethsaida who worked the Sea of Galilee with his brother Andrew. Jesus called him to follow, gave him the name Cephas, “Rock” (Peter), and said: “Upon this rock I will build my Church... I will give you the keys of the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 16:18-19). He was the first to confess Jesus as the Christ, and the one who denied him three times on the night of the Passion. After the Resurrection the Lord asked him three times “Do you love me?” and charged him: “Feed my sheep” (John 21).

After Pentecost Peter led the Church in Jerusalem, preached the first Christian sermon, received the first Gentile convert, Cornelius, and spoke decisively at the Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15). Ancient witnesses, among them Clement of Rome, Ignatius of Antioch and Irenaeus, agree that he came to Rome, led the Church there and was martyred under Nero, crucified, by tradition upside down at his own request. Excavations under St. Peter’s Basilica found the shrine built over his grave on the Vatican Hill. Two letters of the New Testament bear his name. His reign is traditionally counted from about 30-33 to 64 or 67.
did: Received the keys of the kingdom and the charge to feed Christ’s flock
Led the Apostles and the first Church in Jerusalem
Opened the Church to the Gentiles (Acts 10)
Martyred in Rome under Nero; buried on the Vatican Hill
ic: Peter Paul Rubens, Saint Peter as Pope (Prado); Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page
ia: Saint Peter as Pope, painted by Peter Paul Rubens

name: Linus
sum: The first successor of Peter, probably the Linus greeted by St. Paul.
bio: Irenaeus of Lyons, writing around 180, names Linus as the first bishop of Rome after the Apostles and identifies him with the Linus St. Paul mentions in 2 Timothy 4:21. Almost nothing else is known for certain. The Liber Pontificalis, a much later collection of papal lives, says he came from Tuscany and ruled that women should cover their heads in church, but this cannot be checked. He is honored as a martyr and is named in the Roman Canon of the Mass.
did: First successor of St. Peter in the list of Irenaeus
Named in the Roman Canon (Eucharistic Prayer I)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Anacletus
sum: Third Bishop of Rome, also called Cletus, named in the Roman Canon.
bio: Anacletus, also called Cletus, follows Linus in every ancient list. Later writers sometimes split him into two popes, but the Church has long recognized one man. Tradition says he ordained priests for the growing Roman community and was buried near St. Peter. He is commemorated as Cletus in the Roman Canon of the Mass.
did: Named in the Roman Canon as Cletus
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Clement I
sum: Author of the earliest Christian writing outside the New Testament, the Letter to the Corinthians.
bio: Clement is the first Bishop of Rome whose own words survive. Around 96 he wrote to the Church in Corinth, which had deposed its presbyters, urging peace, order and obedience to lawful leaders. The letter was so respected that it was read in some churches alongside Scripture. It also gives early testimony to the martyrdoms of Peter and Paul in Rome. A later tradition says he was exiled to the Crimea and martyred there; St. Cyril, the apostle of the Slavs, brought relics believed to be his back to Rome, where they rest in the Basilica of San Clemente.
did: Wrote the First Letter of Clement to the Corinthians (c. 96)
Witness to the Roman martyrdom of Peter and Paul
Named in the Roman Canon
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Evaristus
bp: Bethlehem, by tradition (of Greek Jewish family)
sum: Fourth successor of Peter, honored as a martyr.
bio: Evaristus appears in all the early lists of Roman bishops, but little is known of his life. The Liber Pontificalis says he was the son of a Greek-speaking Jew from Bethlehem and divided Rome’s titular churches among the priests, which is probably a later author’s guess at the origins of the parish system.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Alexander I
sum: Early Bishop of Rome to whom tradition credits the blessing of holy water.
bio: Irenaeus lists Alexander as the fifth successor of Peter. Later tradition credits him with adding the words of the Institution narrative to the Mass and with blessing water mixed with salt for homes, customs that probably grew up over time rather than by one decree. He is venerated as a martyr, though he is no longer confused with a different Roman martyr Alexander buried on the Via Nomentana.
ic: Alekjds, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Sixtus I
sum: Sixth successor of Peter, honored as a martyr.
bio: Sixtus (in Greek, Xystus) is named in the earliest lists of popes. Later tradition said he ordered that the sacred vessels be handled only by clergy and that the Sanctus be sung at Mass. Nothing further is known with certainty.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Telesphorus
sum: The one early pope whose martyrdom is attested by Irenaeus.
bio: Telesphorus is the only second-century Bishop of Rome whose martyrdom is recorded by Irenaeus, who says he “bore witness gloriously.” Later tradition, which cannot be confirmed, credits him with a Christmas midnight Mass and with a seven-week Lenten fast. Irenaeus also notes that he kept peace with Christians who celebrated Easter on a different date.
did: Martyrdom recorded by St. Irenaeus
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Hyginus
sum: Pope when the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo came to Rome.
bio: According to Irenaeus, the Gnostic teachers Valentinus and Cerdo arrived in Rome during Hyginus’ time, opening a long struggle over true and false teaching. Later tradition says he was a philosopher from Athens and that he organized the ranks of the clergy and introduced godparents at Baptism.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pius I
sum: Brother of the author of the Shepherd of Hermas; faced the heretic Marcion.
bio: The Muratorian Fragment, an early list of Scripture, says that the Shepherd of Hermas was written by Hermas, brother of Pius, while Pius was bishop in Rome. During his time the shipowner Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and the God of Israel, was expelled from the Roman Church (around 144). St. Justin Martyr was teaching in Rome in these years.
did: Marcion was excommunicated by the Roman Church in his time (c. 144)

name: Anicetus
sum: Received St. Polycarp in Rome and kept peace despite their different Easter dates.
bio: Anicetus welcomed the aged bishop Polycarp of Smyrna, a disciple of the Apostle John, around 155. They could not agree on the date of Easter (the churches of Asia kept it on the 14th of Nisan), but Irenaeus records that they parted in peace and that Anicetus let Polycarp celebrate the Eucharist in his place. During his time the historian Hegesippus visited Rome to collect the succession of its bishops.
did: Received St. Polycarp of Smyrna (c. 155)
Kept communion despite the Easter dispute
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Soter
sum: Known for the generous charity of the Roman Church toward other churches.
bio: A letter of Bishop Dionysius of Corinth, quoted by Eusebius, praises Soter and the Roman Church for sending help to poor Christians and those condemned to the mines, and says that a letter from Soter was read aloud in Corinth. Some historians think the yearly celebration of Easter on a Sunday became fixed in Rome in his time.
did: Praised for the Roman Church’s charity to other churches
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Eleutherius
sum: Pope when the Montanist movement and the martyrs of Lyon reached Rome.
bio: Eleutherius had been a deacon under Anicetus. Irenaeus came to Rome during his reign carrying a letter from the martyrs of Lyon about the Montanist movement in Asia Minor. A later legend says a British king named Lucius asked him for missionaries; most historians doubt it.

name: Victor I
sum: The first Latin-speaking pope from Africa; insisted on Easter on Sunday.
bio: Victor, from Roman Africa, was the first Bishop of Rome known to have written in Latin rather than Greek. He pressed the churches of Asia to celebrate Easter on Sunday like the rest of the Church and threatened to cut them off from communion when they refused; Irenaeus urged him toward patience. He also excommunicated Theodotus the Tanner, who taught that Jesus was a mere man.
did: Insisted on Sunday Easter across the Church
Excommunicated Theodotus the Tanner, an early Adoptionist
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Zephyrinus
bur: Catacomb of Callixtus area, Via Appia
sum: Led the Roman Church through debates on the Trinity, with Callixtus as his deacon.
bio: Zephyrinus led the Church during long arguments over the Trinity, when Monarchian teachers blurred the distinction between Father and Son. His chief deacon Callixtus managed the new Christian cemetery on the Via Appia. The theologian Hippolytus, who opposed both men, gives a hostile account of his reign.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Callixtus I
sum: A former slave who became pope and defended mercy toward repentant sinners.
bio: Callixtus had been a slave, a failed banker and a convict in the Sardinian mines before he became deacon to Zephyrinus and administrator of the cemetery on the Via Appia that still bears his name. As pope he admitted to penance and communion sinners who had committed grave sins, and accepted marriages between free women and slaves. Hippolytus attacked his leniency and set himself up as a rival bishop. Callixtus died in Rome, probably in a riot, and is honored as a martyr.
did: Managed the Catacomb of St. Callixtus, the main early papal burial place
Defended the forgiveness of grave sins through penance
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Urban I
sum: Governed the Church in a time of relative peace under Emperor Alexander Severus.
bio: Urban’s reign fell under Emperor Alexander Severus, when Christians lived in relative peace. The rival community of Hippolytus continued. Later legends linked him to the story of St. Cecilia, but these date from long after his time.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pontian
sum: The first pope known to have resigned, exiled to the mines of Sardinia.
bio: In 235 Emperor Maximinus Thrax exiled Pontian and the rival bishop Hippolytus to the mines of Sardinia, a sentence few survived. Pontian resigned on 28 September 235 so that Rome could elect a new bishop, the first precise date in papal history. Tradition holds that he and Hippolytus were reconciled in exile, which healed the schism. Both died there and are honored together as martyrs; Pope Fabian brought Pontian’s body back to Rome.
did: First pope known to have resigned (235)
Reconciled with Hippolytus, ending Rome’s first schism
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Anterus
sum: Reigned only about six weeks; his tomb was found in the papal crypt.
bio: Anterus reigned only a few weeks. Tradition says he collected the acts of the martyrs for the Roman archives, and that this cost him his life. His tomb, with a Greek inscription bearing his name, was found in the Crypt of the Popes in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus in 1854.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Fabian
bur: Catacomb of Callixtus; relics at San Sebastiano
sum: A layman chosen when a dove settled on his head; martyred under Decius.
bio: Eusebius tells that Fabian, a layman who had come into the city, was chosen when a dove settled on his head during the election. He divided Rome into seven districts, each under a deacon, and built up the cemeteries. He was one of the first victims of the persecution of Emperor Decius and died on 20 January 250. His tombstone survives in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus. St. Cyprian called him an “incomparable man.”
did: Organized Rome into seven deaconries
Martyred in the Decian persecution (250)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Cornelius
sum: Upheld mercy for Christians who had lapsed under persecution, against Novatian.
bio: After the persecution of Decius, Cornelius was elected over the priest Novatian, who refused forgiveness to Christians who had lapsed under torture and set himself up as a rival bishop. Supported by St. Cyprian of Carthage, Cornelius held a synod that allowed the lapsed back after penance. A letter of his gives a rare picture of the Roman clergy at the time: 46 priests, 7 deacons and over 1,500 widows and poor supported by the Church. He died in exile at Centumcellae (Civitavecchia) and is named with Cyprian in the Roman Canon.
did: Reconciled the lapsed after penance, against the rigorist Novatian
His letter describes the size of the Roman Church in 251
Named in the Roman Canon
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Lucius I
sum: Exiled soon after his election; continued Cornelius’ mercy toward the lapsed.
bio: Lucius was exiled shortly after his election under Emperor Gallus and returned when the persecution eased. St. Cyprian wrote to congratulate him and praised him for continuing his predecessor’s policy toward the lapsed. His tombstone was found in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen I
sum: Defended the validity of baptism given by heretics against Cyprian.
bio: Stephen held that people baptized by heretics with the right form were truly baptized and should not be baptized again, only received with the laying on of hands. St. Cyprian of Carthage and Firmilian of Caesarea disagreed sharply. The Church later confirmed Stephen’s position. The story that he was beheaded in his chair is a later legend.
did: Taught that valid baptism by heretics must not be repeated, the Church’s lasting teaching
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sixtus II
sum: Beheaded while preaching in the catacombs, with four of his deacons; St. Lawrence followed days later.
bio: Sixtus restored good relations with Carthage after the baptism dispute. Under Emperor Valerian’s edict against the clergy he was seized while seated in his chair, teaching the faithful in the Catacomb of Praetextatus, and beheaded on 6 August 258 with four deacons. His deacon St. Lawrence was martyred four days later. He was one of the most venerated martyrs of Rome and is named in the Roman Canon.
did: Martyred under Valerian (258)
Named in the Roman Canon
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Dionysius
sum: Rebuilt the Roman Church after Valerian’s persecution and clarified teaching on the Trinity.
bio: Dionysius was elected after a long vacancy caused by persecution. When Emperor Gallienus granted toleration, he reorganized the Roman Church and its cemeteries. He wrote to his namesake Dionysius of Alexandria asking him to clarify his language about the Son, an important step in the Church’s thinking on the Trinity. He also sent money to ransom Christians in Cappadocia taken captive by the Goths.
did: Wrote on the Trinity against both Sabellianism and tritheism
Ransomed Christian captives in Cappadocia
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Felix I
sum: Wrote on the divinity and humanity of Christ.
bio: Felix wrote a letter on the unity of the person of Christ, true God and true man, part of which was quoted at the Council of Ephesus (431), though its authenticity is debated. During his reign the bishops of the East deposed Paul of Samosata, and Emperor Aurelian ruled that the church building in Antioch belonged to the bishop in communion with Rome.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Eutychian
sum: Pope in a quiet time before the Great Persecution.
bio: Eutychian led the Church in a time of peace. Parts of his epitaph were found in the papal crypt of St. Callixtus. Later stories credit him with personally burying hundreds of martyrs and blessing crops, but they come from much later sources.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Caius
sum: Said by tradition to be a relative of Emperor Diocletian.
bio: Caius (Gaius) governed the Church in the years before the Great Persecution. Tradition, not confirmed, makes him a Dalmatian and a relative of Diocletian, and says he set the grades of ordination a man must pass through before becoming a bishop. His tomb was found in the Catacomb of St. Callixtus.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Marcellinus
sum: Pope during the Great Persecution of Diocletian.
bio: Marcellinus led the Church when Diocletian’s Great Persecution began in 303, with orders to burn Scripture and destroy churches. Some ancient opponents claimed he offered incense to the gods; others say he repented and was martyred. The Church venerates him as a saint. After his death the see was vacant for several years.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Marcellus I
bur: Catacomb of Priscilla; relics at San Marcello al Corso
sum: Rebuilt the Roman Church after the persecution; exiled for requiring penance of the lapsed.
bio: After a vacancy of several years, Marcellus reorganized the Church in Rome. He insisted that Christians who had lapsed under persecution do penance before readmission, which caused riots, and Emperor Maxentius exiled him. Pope Damasus later wrote an epitaph praising his firmness. The church of San Marcello al Corso is said to stand on the site where he was forced to work in the imperial stables.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Eusebius
sum: Exiled to Sicily after a few months over the same dispute about the lapsed.
bio: Eusebius kept the policy of penance for the lapsed, which led to more disorder. Emperor Maxentius exiled both him and his opponent Heraclius. He died in Sicily after a reign of about four months. Pope Damasus’ epitaph for him survives in copies.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Miltiades
sum: Saw the end of persecution and received the Lateran palace from Constantine.
bio: Miltiades was pope when Constantine won the Battle of the Milvian Bridge (312) and the Edict of Milan (313) granted Christians freedom of worship and the return of their property. Constantine gave the Church the Lateran palace, which became the papal residence for a thousand years. In 313 Miltiades presided over a synod in the Lateran on the Donatist schism in Africa.
did: Saw the Edict of Milan (313) end the persecution
Received the Lateran palace from Constantine
Held the Lateran synod on the Donatist schism (313)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sylvester I
bur: Catacomb of Priscilla; relics at San Silvestro in Capite
sum: Pope during the reign of Constantine, the Council of Nicaea and the first great basilicas.
bio: Sylvester governed the Church for over twenty years, during which Constantine built the first great churches of Rome: the Lateran Basilica, Old St. Peter’s over the Apostle’s tomb, and others. The First Council of Nicaea (325), which defined that the Son is “consubstantial with the Father” against Arius, met in his time; he did not attend but sent two priests as legates. The famous legends that he baptized Constantine and received the “Donation of Constantine” are later inventions; the Donation was exposed as a forgery in the fifteenth century.
did: First Council of Nicaea (325) met during his reign; represented by legates
Lateran Basilica and Old St. Peter’s built in his time
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Mark
bur: Catacomb of Balbina; relics at San Marco, Rome
sum: Founded the Basilica of San Marco in Rome.
bio: In his short reign of about nine months Mark built two churches, the basilica that became San Marco in Rome and a cemetery basilica on the Via Ardeatina. The Depositio episcoporum, a list of papal burial dates, begins to give reliable dates in this period.
did: Founded the Basilica of San Marco, Rome
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Julius I
sum: Defended St. Athanasius and the faith of Nicaea against the Arians.
bio: Julius received St. Athanasius of Alexandria and other bishops driven out by the Arians, held a synod in Rome (341) that declared Athanasius innocent, and wrote a firm letter to the Eastern bishops claiming the right of Rome to be consulted. The Council of Serdica (343) recognized appeals to the Bishop of Rome. He built several churches, including the basilica that became Santa Maria in Trastevere. The celebration of Christmas on 25 December is first recorded in Rome around this time.
did: Defended St. Athanasius and the Creed of Nicaea
Council of Serdica (343) recognized appeals to Rome
Built churches including the forerunner of Santa Maria in Trastevere
ic: Hugo DK, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Liberius
sum: Exiled by an Arian emperor for refusing to condemn Athanasius.
bio: Liberius refused Emperor Constantius II’s demand to condemn Athanasius and was exiled to Thrace in 355. Under pressure he later signed an ambiguous formula and was allowed back to Rome, where a rival, Felix II, had been installed. His weakness in exile is debated, but after the Emperor’s death he firmly upheld Nicaea. He is the first pope not venerated as a saint in the West. The legend that he founded Santa Maria Maggiore after a summer snowfall is not historical, though a basilica of his did stand nearby.
did: Exiled for defending Athanasius (355)
Restored the Nicene faith after the Arian crisis
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Damasus I
bur: Via Ardeatina; relics at San Lorenzo in Damaso
sum: Patron of St. Jerome’s Bible, poet of the martyrs, and champion of the Roman See.
bio: Damasus’ election was disputed by a rival party and marred by deadly violence. He went on to make the Roman See a center of learning and authority. He commissioned his secretary St. Jerome to revise the Latin Gospels, the start of the Vulgate. He restored the catacombs and wrote verse epitaphs for the martyrs, carved in beautiful letters by Furius Dionysius Filocalus. The Council of Rome (382) under him is associated with a list of the books of Scripture. In 380 Emperor Theodosius made the faith “of Pope Damasus” the religion of the Empire.
did: Commissioned St. Jerome’s Latin revision of the Bible (the Vulgate)
Restored the catacombs and wrote epitaphs for the martyrs
Council of Rome (382) associated with the canon of Scripture
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Siricius
sum: Author of the oldest surviving papal decretal.
bio: Siricius’ letter of 385 to Bishop Himerius of Tarragona, answering questions on Baptism, penance and clerical life, is the oldest papal decretal that survives: a ruling with the force of law for the wider Church. He required continence of clergy in major orders and condemned the monk Jovinian, who denied the perpetual virginity of Mary. He dedicated the rebuilt Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls in 390.
did: Issued the oldest surviving papal decretal (385)
Condemned Jovinian’s denial of Mary’s perpetual virginity
Dedicated the new Basilica of St. Paul Outside the Walls
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Anastasius I
sum: Condemned certain teachings attributed to Origen; praised by Jerome.
bio: Anastasius condemned the writings of Origen as they were then being circulated in Latin translation and encouraged the African bishops against the Donatists. St. Jerome praised him as a man of “most rich poverty.” He is venerated as a saint.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Innocent I
sum: Pope during the sack of Rome by Alaric; strengthened Roman authority in the West.
bio: Innocent’s many letters claimed for Rome the final word in major disputes. He supported St. John Chrysostom when he was unjustly deposed in Constantinople. He was away at Ravenna seeking help from the Emperor when Alaric’s Goths sacked Rome in 410. He confirmed the African councils’ condemnation of Pelagius, which led St. Augustine to write, in a phrase later summarized as “Rome has spoken, the case is closed,” that the matter was settled. His letter to Decentius of Gubbio is a key early source on the liturgy.
did: Supported St. John Chrysostom
Rome sacked by Alaric’s Goths (410)
Confirmed the condemnation of Pelagianism (417)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Zosimus
sum: Wavered over Pelagius before finally condemning him in his Tractoria.
bio: Zosimus at first reopened the case of Pelagius and Caelestius, angering the African bishops. After the Council of Carthage (418) and an imperial decree, he issued his Epistola Tractoria condemning Pelagianism and sent it to all bishops. His short reign was full of disputes, including a quarrel over the authority of Arles in Gaul.
did: Issued the Epistola Tractoria condemning Pelagianism (418)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Boniface I
sum: Overcame the antipope Eulalius and supported St. Augustine against the Pelagians.
bio: After a double election, Emperor Honorius recognized Boniface over the antipope Eulalius. Boniface backed St. Augustine, who dedicated a work against the Pelagians to him, and he firmly defended the rights of the Roman See in Illyricum against Constantinople.

name: Celestine I
bur: Catacomb of Priscilla; relics at Santa Prassede
sum: Condemned Nestorius and sent his legates to the Council of Ephesus.
bio: Celestine held a Roman synod (430) that condemned Nestorius, who refused to call Mary Theotokos, Mother of God, and entrusted the case to St. Cyril of Alexandria. His legates took part in the Council of Ephesus (431), which upheld Mary as Mother of God. He sent Palladius as the first bishop “to the Irish believing in Christ,” shortly before St. Patrick’s mission, and fought Pelagianism in Britain through St. Germanus.
did: Condemned Nestorius; legates at the Council of Ephesus (431)
Sent Palladius as first bishop to Ireland (431)
ic: Crescens Lajos Dedek, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Sixtus III
sum: Built Santa Maria Maggiore to honor Mary as Mother of God after Ephesus.
bio: Sixtus helped reconcile Cyril of Alexandria and John of Antioch after the Council of Ephesus (433). He built the Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, whose mosaics celebrating Mary as Mother of God survive, and the octagonal baptistery of the Lateran in its present form. He also founded the first monastery at the Vatican.
did: Built Santa Maria Maggiore with its surviving fifth-century mosaics
Helped reconcile Cyril and John of Antioch (433)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo I
sum: “Leo the Great”: his Tome guided the Council of Chalcedon, and he met Attila in 452.
bio: Leo was a deacon of great influence before his election. His Tome to Flavian (449) set out the faith in one Person of Christ in two natures, divine and human; at the Council of Chalcedon (451) the bishops cried out, “Peter has spoken through Leo!” In 452 he met Attila the Hun near Mantua and persuaded him to withdraw from Italy, and in 455 he obtained from the Vandal king Gaiseric that Rome would not be burned or its people massacred. Nearly a hundred of his sermons and over 140 letters survive; they shaped the Roman liturgy and the theology of the papacy as the office of Peter. He is a Doctor of the Church.
did: Tome of Leo defined Christ’s two natures; adopted at Chalcedon (451)
Persuaded Attila to withdraw from Italy (452)
Doctor of the Church; first pope called “the Great”
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Hilarius
sum: Legate at the “Robber Synod” of Ephesus who escaped to tell the tale; later a strong pope.
bio: As Leo’s legate at the “Robber Synod” of Ephesus (449), Hilarius protested the deposition of Flavian and fled for his life, later giving thanks in an oratory at the Lateran baptistery dedicated to St. John the Evangelist. As pope he upheld church order in Gaul and Spain and built churches and libraries at the Lateran.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Simplicius
sum: Pope when the Western Roman Empire fell in 476.
bio: In 476 the last Western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed by Odoacer, and Simplicius was left as a leading authority in Italy. He resisted the Monophysite party in the East and the attempt of Constantinople to rank itself above other ancient sees. He built Santo Stefano Rotondo on the Caelian Hill.
did: Saw the end of the Western Roman Empire (476)
Built Santo Stefano Rotondo

name: Felix III
sum: Excommunicated Patriarch Acacius, beginning the 35-year Acacian Schism.
bio: Felix (sometimes numbered Felix II) was from a Roman senatorial family and an ancestor of Pope Gregory the Great. He rejected the Henotikon, an imperial formula that sidestepped Chalcedon, and in 484 excommunicated Patriarch Acacius of Constantinople, opening the first long break between Rome and Constantinople.
did: Excommunicated Acacius of Constantinople (484), the Acacian Schism
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gelasius I
sum: Set out the “two powers” that govern the world: priestly authority and royal power.
bio: Gelasius wrote to Emperor Anastasius in 494 that “two there are by which this world is chiefly ruled: the sacred authority of bishops and the royal power,” a letter that shaped medieval thought on Church and State. He cared for refugees and the poor during famine, opposed the pagan Lupercalia festival, and wrote widely. The Gelasian Sacramentary bears his name, though it was compiled later.
did: Letter Duo sunt on spiritual and temporal power (494)
Ended the Lupercalia festival in Rome
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Anastasius II
sum: Sought to heal the Acacian Schism; Dante placed him in hell by mistake.
bio: Anastasius tried to end the schism with Constantinople by gentler means, which upset some Roman clergy. Medieval writers wrongly believed he had fallen into heresy, and Dante placed him in the Inferno, confusing him with the Emperor of the same name. Clovis, king of the Franks, was baptized during his reign (c. 496).
did: Clovis of the Franks baptized in his time (c. 496)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Symmachus
sum: Survived the Laurentian Schism; a synod declared that no one may judge the pope.
bio: A convert from paganism, Symmachus was elected the same day as the rival Laurentius, and years of street fighting followed. King Theodoric first recognized Symmachus. When enemies accused him of crimes, a synod (501) refused to judge him, holding that the Apostolic See is judged by no one. He was generous to the poor and to exiled African bishops, and built at St. Peter’s.
did: Ended the Laurentian Schism
Synod of 501: the pope is judged by no one
ic: José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Hormisdas
sum: Ended the Acacian Schism with the Formula of Hormisdas, signed by the Eastern bishops.
bio: Hormisdas, a widower and father of the future Pope Silverius, ended the 35-year Acacian Schism in 519. Emperor Justin I and the bishops of the East signed his Formula, which states that “in the Apostolic See the Catholic religion has always been kept unblemished.” The First Vatican Council quoted it in 1870.
did: Formula of Hormisdas ended the Acacian Schism (519)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John I
sum: Sent to Constantinople by Theodoric; died in his prison at Ravenna.
bio: The Arian Ostrogothic king Theodoric forced John to go to Constantinople to plead for Arians there, the first pope to visit the city, where he was received with great honor. On his return Theodoric, suspecting treason, imprisoned him at Ravenna, where he died of hardship. He is venerated as a martyr. The philosopher Boethius was put to death by Theodoric in the same years.
did: First pope to visit Constantinople (526)
Died in Theodoric’s prison; venerated as a martyr

name: Felix IV
sum: Turned Roman buildings in the Forum into the Basilica of Sts. Cosmas and Damian.
bio: Felix (sometimes numbered Felix III) was imposed by Theodoric but governed well. He converted two buildings in the Roman Forum into the Church of Sts. Cosmas and Damian, the first church in the Forum, with a famous apse mosaic. He approved the canons of the Council of Orange (529) on grace. Before dying he tried to name his own successor, which caused a disputed election.
did: Founded Sts. Cosmas and Damian in the Forum
Confirmed the Council of Orange on grace (529)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Boniface II
sum: The first pope of Germanic descent.
bio: Boniface was a Roman of Gothic family, chosen by his predecessor. A majority elected Dioscorus instead, but he died within weeks. Boniface confirmed the Council of Orange’s teaching against semi-Pelagianism.

name: John II
sum: The first pope to take a new name, since his own was that of a pagan god.
bio: Born Mercurius, after the Roman god Mercury, he chose the name John on election, the first pope known to change his name. He received Emperor Justinian’s confession of faith, including the phrase “one of the Trinity suffered in the flesh.”
did: First pope to take a papal name

name: Agapetus I
sum: Deposed the Monophysite Patriarch Anthimus in Constantinople.
bio: Sent by the Gothic king to Constantinople to prevent Justinian’s invasion of Italy, Agapetus failed in that mission but persuaded the Emperor to depose the Monophysite Patriarch Anthimus. He consecrated the orthodox Menas in his place and died in Constantinople. With Cassiodorus he had planned a Christian school in Rome.
did: Deposed Patriarch Anthimus and consecrated Menas (536)

name: Silverius
sum: Son of Pope Hormisdas; deposed by Belisarius at the bidding of Empress Theodora.
bio: Silverius was the son of Pope Hormisdas, born before his father’s ordination. The Byzantine general Belisarius, taking Rome, accused him of conspiring with the Goths and deposed him in 537, reportedly at the wish of Empress Theodora, who favored the deacon Vigilius. He died of starvation and ill-treatment on the island of Palmarola and is honored as a martyr; he is patron of the island of Ponza.
did: Deposed by Belisarius and died in exile (537)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Vigilius
sum: Held in Constantinople for years by Justinian during the Three Chapters dispute.
bio: Vigilius owed his election to imperial favor, but once pope he resisted the Emperor. Justinian brought him to Constantinople, where he was held for about eight years under pressure to condemn the “Three Chapters,” writings judged sympathetic to Nestorianism. He wavered, and finally approved the Second Council of Constantinople (553). He died in Syracuse on the way home.
did: Second Council of Constantinople (553) met in his reign
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pelagius I
sum: Restored order and relief in Rome after the Gothic War.
bio: Pelagius had saved Rome from destruction by negotiating with the Gothic king Totila. Chosen by Justinian, he was at first mistrusted for accepting the Council of 553, and swore publicly at St. Peter’s that he had done nothing against the faith. He reorganized church finances, fed the poor and ransomed captives after the devastation of the war.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John III
sum: Pope during the Lombard invasion of Italy.
bio: John (born Catelinus) reigned as the Lombards invaded Italy in 568. He sought help from the Byzantine general Narses, restored the catacombs and completed the Church of the Holy Apostles in Rome. Few of his acts survive because of the disorder of the times.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict I
sum: Reigned during the Lombard siege and famine in Rome.
bio: Benedict’s election had to wait almost a year for confirmation from Constantinople. Rome was besieged by the Lombards and short of food; the Emperor sent grain ships from Egypt. He died during the siege.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pelagius II
sum: Rebuilt San Lorenzo and sent the deacon Gregory to Constantinople; died of the plague.
bio: Elected during a Lombard siege, Pelagius sent the deacon Gregory (the future Gregory the Great) as his envoy to Constantinople. He objected to the Patriarch of Constantinople’s title “Ecumenical Patriarch,” rebuilt the Basilica of San Lorenzo fuori le Mura with its mosaic, and died in the plague of 590.
did: Rebuilt San Lorenzo fuori le Mura
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory I
sum: “Gregory the Great”: monk, pastor, writer, and sender of the mission to England.
bio: Gregory came from a wealthy Roman family and served as prefect of the city before giving his property to found monasteries and becoming a monk. As pope he fed Rome through famine and plague, negotiated with the Lombards when the Empire could not, and organized the estates of the Church to support the poor. In 596 he sent St. Augustine of Canterbury and forty monks to convert the English. His Pastoral Rule shaped bishops for a thousand years; his Dialogues tell of St. Benedict; his Moralia comment on Job. He called himself “servant of the servants of God.” Gregorian chant is named after him, though it took its final form later. He is a Doctor of the Church.
did: Sent St. Augustine of Canterbury to England (596)
Wrote the Pastoral Rule, Dialogues and Moralia on Job
Organized relief for Rome’s poor; negotiated peace with the Lombards
Doctor of the Church; took the title “servant of the servants of God”
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sabinian
sum: Sold grain from the Church’s stores during a famine, which made him unpopular.
bio: Sabinian had been Gregory’s envoy in Constantinople. In a famine he sold grain from the Church’s granaries instead of giving it away as Gregory had, and was so unpopular that his funeral procession had to avoid the city center. A late tradition says he ordered bells rung at the canonical hours.

name: Boniface III
sum: Obtained an imperial decree that Rome was the head of all the churches.
bio: As envoy to Constantinople, Boniface had won the favor of Emperor Phocas, who issued a decree recognizing the Apostolic See of Peter as head of all churches. As pope he held a synod forbidding discussion of a successor while a pope was alive. He reigned under nine months.

name: Boniface IV
sum: Turned the Pantheon into a church dedicated to Mary and all the martyrs.
bio: With the permission of Emperor Phocas, Boniface consecrated the Pantheon as the Church of St. Mary and the Martyrs in 609, the first pagan temple in Rome turned into a church, which saved the building. He corresponded with St. Columbanus and met Mellitus, Bishop of London.
did: Consecrated the Pantheon as a church (609)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Adeodatus I
sum: A priest of long service who cared for victims of earthquake and plague.
bio: Deusdedit (Adeodatus) was the first priest elected pope in a long time, after several deacons. He favored the Roman clergy, cared for the sick during an earthquake and an outbreak of disease, and left a gift to the clergy in his will. The oldest surviving papal lead seal (bulla) is his.
did: Oldest surviving papal lead seal
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Boniface V
sum: Encouraged the mission in England and confirmed churches as places of sanctuary.
bio: Boniface wrote to King Edwin of Northumbria and his Christian queen Ethelburga encouraging Edwin’s conversion, and gave the pallium to Justus of Canterbury. He confirmed the right of asylum in churches.

name: Honorius I
sum: Able administrator later condemned for his careless letter on Monothelitism.
bio: Honorius was an able pastor who supported the English mission, restored churches (including Sant’Agnese fuori le Mura with its mosaic) and roofed St. Peter’s with bronze tiles. In a letter to Patriarch Sergius he wrote of “one will” in Christ, a phrase used by the Monothelite heresy. The Third Council of Constantinople (681) anathematized him, and Pope Leo II confirmed it as negligence in suppressing heresy. The case was much discussed at the First Vatican Council.
did: Rebuilt Sant’Agnese fuori le Mura
Condemned by the Third Council of Constantinople for his letter on “one will”
ic: José Luiz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Severinus
sum: Waited almost two years for imperial approval and reigned only two months.
bio: Severinus was elected in 638 but approval from Constantinople was withheld because he would not sign the Ecthesis, Emperor Heraclius’ Monothelite decree. Meanwhile imperial officials plundered the Lateran treasury. He was finally consecrated in May 640 and died two months later.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John IV
sum: Dalmatian pope who condemned Monothelitism and ransomed captives.
bio: John condemned the Ecthesis and Monothelitism at a Roman synod. He sent money to ransom Christians captured by Slavic invaders in his native Dalmatia and Istria and brought relics of Dalmatian martyrs to Rome, building the chapel of San Venanzio at the Lateran.
did: Condemned Monothelitism (641)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Theodore I
sum: Greek pope from Jerusalem who opposed Monothelitism.
bio: Theodore, son of a bishop from Jerusalem, continued resistance to Monothelitism, excommunicating Patriarch Pyrrhus and then Patriarch Paul of Constantinople. He welcomed St. Maximus the Confessor and prepared the Lateran Synod held by his successor.

name: Martin I
sum: Condemned Monothelitism at the Lateran Synod and died in exile in Crimea.
bio: Martin was consecrated without waiting for imperial approval and at once held the Lateran Synod of 649 with St. Maximus the Confessor, condemning Monothelitism and the Emperor’s decree, the Typos. Emperor Constans II had him arrested in 653, carried to Constantinople, tried, publicly humiliated and exiled to Chersonesus in Crimea, where he died of hunger and cold. He is the last pope venerated as a martyr.
did: Lateran Synod (649) condemned Monothelitism
Arrested, tried and exiled by Constans II; last martyr pope
ic: Enric, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Eugene I
sum: Elected while Martin I was still alive in exile.
bio: Under imperial pressure the Roman clergy elected Eugene while Martin was in exile; Martin seems to have accepted it. Eugene refused a compromise letter from the Patriarch of Constantinople, which the Roman people shouted down in church, and he was spared Martin’s fate only by the Emperor’s war with the Arabs.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Vitalian
sum: Sent Theodore of Tarsus to Canterbury, who organized the English Church.
bio: Vitalian kept peace with Constantinople and received Emperor Constans II in Rome in 663, who then stripped the city of bronze. In 668 he sent the learned Greek monk Theodore of Tarsus, with Abbot Hadrian, to be Archbishop of Canterbury; Theodore organized the English Church. After the Synod of Whitby (664) England followed Roman practice on Easter.
did: Sent Theodore of Tarsus to Canterbury (668)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Adeodatus II
sum: Former monk of St. Erasmus, generous to pilgrims.
bio: Adeodatus had been a monk at St. Erasmus on the Caelian Hill and enlarged that monastery. He was known for kindness to pilgrims and the poor and opposed Monothelitism. He is sometimes counted as a saint in local tradition.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Donus
sum: Ended the claim of Ravenna to be independent of Rome.
bio: Donus paved the atrium of St. Peter’s with marble and saw the Archbishop of Ravenna drop his claim to independence from Rome. He discovered and dispersed a community of Nestorian monks in Rome.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Agatho
sum: His letter guided the Third Council of Constantinople, which ended Monothelitism.
bio: Agatho, a Sicilian monk, sent legates to the Third Council of Constantinople (680-681) with a dogmatic letter stating that Christ has two wills, divine and human, in harmony. The council accepted it, saying that “Peter spoke through Agatho.” He also heard the appeal of St. Wilfrid of York.
did: Letter on the two wills of Christ accepted at Constantinople III (680-681)
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Leo II
sum: Confirmed the Third Council of Constantinople, including the condemnation of Honorius.
bio: A skilled singer and Greek scholar, Leo approved the acts of the Third Council of Constantinople and translated them into Latin. He specified that Honorius was condemned for not suppressing heresy. He also ended the practice of the Archbishop of Ravenna paying fees for his pallium.
did: Confirmed the Third Council of Constantinople

name: Benedict II
sum: Won from the Emperor the right to consecrate popes without waiting for approval.
bio: Benedict waited nearly a year for imperial confirmation. He then obtained from Emperor Constantine IV a decree allowing a newly elected pope to be consecrated immediately, with approval from the exarch at Ravenna. He worked to win back the Monothelite Patriarch Macarius.

name: John V
sum: The first of a series of Eastern popes, and the first consecrated without imperial approval.
bio: John was a Syrian who had served as a legate at the Third Council of Constantinople. He was the first pope consecrated under the new rule without waiting for the Emperor, and he obtained tax relief for church estates in Sicily and Calabria. He was ill for most of his short reign.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Conon
sum: A compromise candidate who received the Irish missionary St. Kilian.
bio: Conon, son of a soldier, was chosen as a compromise between the clergy and the army. He was elderly and ill but received the Irish missionary Kilian and sent him to preach in Franconia, where he was later martyred.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sergius I
sum: Added the Agnus Dei to the Mass and rejected the Quinisext Council.
bio: Sergius refused to sign the canons of the Quinisext Council (692), which condemned some Roman practices; when the Emperor sent an officer to arrest him, Roman and Ravennese soldiers protected him. He added the Agnus Dei to the Mass, introduced processions for Marian feasts, baptized the Saxon king Caedwalla and consecrated St. Willibrord as bishop for the Frisians.
did: Added the Agnus Dei to the Mass
Rejected the Quinisext Council (692)
Consecrated St. Willibrord, apostle of the Frisians
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John VI
sum: Protected the imperial exarch from mutinous troops and ransomed captives.
bio: John, a Greek, shielded the exarch Theophylact from Italian soldiers who rose against him and paid the Lombard duke of Benevento to free prisoners. He also heard St. Wilfrid of York’s appeal again and restored him.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John VII
sum: Son of a Byzantine official, patron of art at Santa Maria Antiqua.
bio: John, son of a Byzantine official, decorated Santa Maria Antiqua in the Forum with frescoes that survive and built an oratory to the Virgin at St. Peter’s. He handled the Quinisext canons cautiously, returning them to Justinian II without signing.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sisinnius
sum: Reigned just three weeks, so crippled by gout he could not feed himself.
bio: Sisinnius, a Syrian, was so ill with gout that he could not feed himself, yet in his twenty days as pope he ordered lime prepared to repair Rome’s walls and consecrated a bishop for Corsica.

name: Constantine
sum: Traveled to Constantinople, the last pope to visit the city until Paul VI in 1967.
bio: Constantine was summoned by Justinian II and went to Constantinople in 710-711. The Emperor received him with honor, kissed his feet, and settled the dispute over the Quinisext Council. No pope visited Constantinople again until Paul VI went to Istanbul in 1967. He resisted the Monothelite Emperor Philippicus after Justinian’s death.
did: Last pope to visit Constantinople for over 1,250 years (710-711)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory II
sum: Sent St. Boniface to Germany and resisted the iconoclast Emperor Leo III.
bio: Gregory, a Roman, restored the walls of Rome and rebuilt Monte Cassino. In 719 he gave the English monk Winfrid the name Boniface and sent him to preach in Germany, later making him a bishop. When Emperor Leo III ordered the destruction of icons (726), Gregory refused, defending the veneration of images, while restraining Italians who wanted to revolt against the Empire.
did: Sent St. Boniface as apostle to Germany (719)
Defended holy images against iconoclasm
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory III
sum: Condemned iconoclasm; the last pope born outside Europe until Francis.
bio: Gregory held a synod in 731 excommunicating those who destroyed holy images. The Emperor in reply seized papal estates in southern Italy and Sicily. Facing the Lombards, he asked the Frankish leader Charles Martel for help, a first step toward the papal alliance with the Franks. He was the last pope born outside Europe until Francis in 2013.
did: Roman synod condemning iconoclasm (731)
Last non-European pope until 2013
ic: ASKI, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Zachary
sum: Approved Pepin as king of the Franks and talked Lombard kings out of war.
bio: Zachary, the last Greek pope, personally persuaded the Lombard kings Liutprand and Ratchis to give up conquered territory and make peace. Asked whether the man with royal power or the powerless Merovingian should be king of the Franks, he answered in favor of Pepin the Short, who was crowned in 751. He supported St. Boniface’s reform of the Frankish Church and translated Gregory’s Dialogues into Greek.
did: Supported Pepin’s kingship (751)
Made peace with the Lombards by personal diplomacy

name: Stephen II
sum: Crossed the Alps to win Pepin’s help; the Donation of Pepin founded the Papal States.
bio: A priest named Stephen was elected in March 752 but died three or four days later, before his consecration. Older lists counted him as Stephen II; since 1961 the Vatican lists do not, which is why later Stephens carry double numbers, such as Stephen II (III). The Stephen elected next faced the Lombard king Aistulf, who had taken Ravenna. He crossed the Alps in winter, the first pope to do so, anointed Pepin and his sons at Saint-Denis, and Pepin defeated the Lombards and gave the conquered lands to the pope. This Donation of Pepin (756) was the beginning of the Papal States, which lasted until 1870.
did: Donation of Pepin (756), origin of the Papal States
First pope to cross the Alps; anointed Pepin at Saint-Denis (754)

name: Paul I
sum: Brother of Stephen II; moved martyrs’ relics from the catacombs into the city.
bio: Paul, younger brother of Stephen II, kept the Frankish alliance and protected the new Papal States from the Lombards and from Constantinople. Because the catacombs were being raided, he moved many martyrs’ relics into Roman churches and turned his family home into the monastery of San Silvestro in Capite.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen III
sum: Held the Lateran Synod of 769, which barred laymen from becoming pope.
bio: Stephen was elected after the violent intrusion of the antipope Constantine II, a layman. His Lateran Synod of 769 ruled that only cardinal priests or deacons could be elected and that laymen had no vote, and it condemned iconoclasm. Some of the antipope’s supporters were blinded in the unrest, which shadowed his reign. He is also numbered Stephen IV.
did: Lateran Synod of 769 on papal elections and holy images
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Adrian I
sum: Ally of Charlemagne; approved the Second Council of Nicaea on holy images.
bio: Adrian, a Roman noble, called on Charlemagne, who destroyed the Lombard kingdom in 774 and confirmed the papal lands. He restored Rome’s aqueducts, walls and churches and set up farm estates to feed the poor. His legates attended the Second Council of Nicaea (787), which restored the veneration of icons. Charlemagne wrote an epitaph for him, still in St. Peter’s. His reign of almost 24 years was the longest after St. Peter’s until Pius VI in the late eighteenth century.
did: Alliance with Charlemagne; end of the Lombard kingdom (774)
Approved the Second Council of Nicaea (787)
Restored Rome’s aqueducts and walls

name: Leo III
sum: Crowned Charlemagne emperor on Christmas Day 800.
bio: Leo was attacked in a Roman street in 799 by relatives of his predecessor, who tried to blind him and cut out his tongue. He escaped to Charlemagne, who restored him. On Christmas Day 800, in St. Peter’s, Leo crowned Charlemagne Emperor of the Romans, founding what became the Holy Roman Empire. He refused Charlemagne’s wish to add the Filioque to the Creed, though he agreed with its teaching, and had the Creed engraved without it on silver shields.
did: Crowned Charlemagne emperor (800)
Kept the Creed without the Filioque in Rome
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen IV
sum: Crowned Louis the Pious emperor at Reims.
bio: Stephen traveled to Reims in 816 to crown Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, and to renew the alliance. He died soon after returning. He is also numbered Stephen V.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Paschal I
sum: Builder of Santa Prassede and Santa Cecilia, with their brilliant mosaics.
bio: Paschal obtained from Louis the Pious the Pactum Ludovicianum confirming papal lands. He rebuilt Santa Prassede, with the chapel of St. Zeno and its gold mosaics, Santa Cecilia in Trastevere, where he placed the saint’s relics, and Santa Maria in Domnica. He sheltered Greek monks fleeing iconoclasm. His harsh rule in Rome made him unpopular, but he is venerated as a saint.
did: Built Santa Prassede, Santa Cecilia and Santa Maria in Domnica
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Eugene II
sum: Accepted the Constitutio Romana, giving the emperor oversight of papal elections.
bio: Eugene’s election was backed by the nobility and Emperor Lothair. The Constitutio Romana (824) required a newly elected pope to swear loyalty to the emperor before consecration. His Roman synod of 826 called for schools at cathedrals and parishes.

name: Valentine
sum: Reigned about forty days.
bio: Valentine, a well-liked Roman deacon, was chosen unanimously and died about forty days later. Little else is known of him.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory IV
sum: Promoted All Saints’ Day on 1 November and fortified Ostia.
bio: Gregory was drawn into the quarrel between Louis the Pious and his sons and failed as a mediator. He promoted the feast of All Saints on 1 November in the Frankish lands, rebuilt Ostia as Gregoriopolis against Saracen raids and supported St. Ansgar’s mission to Scandinavia.
did: Spread the feast of All Saints on 1 November
Supported St. Ansgar, apostle of the North
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sergius II
sum: Pope when Saracen raiders looted St. Peter’s and St. Paul’s in 846.
bio: Sergius was chosen over a popular deacon and consecrated without imperial approval, which brought Lothair’s army to Rome. His brother Benedict was accused of selling church offices. In 846 Arab raiders sailed up the Tiber and looted St. Peter’s and St. Paul’s, which lay outside the walls.
did: Saracen raid on St. Peter’s and St. Paul’s (846)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo IV
sum: Built the Leonine Wall around the Vatican and won the naval battle of Ostia.
bio: After the raid of 846, Leo built a wall around the Vatican, creating the “Leonine City,” and repaired the city’s defenses. In 849 he blessed an allied fleet that defeated the Saracens at Ostia, a victory painted by Raphael in the Vatican. He welcomed the young Alfred of Wessex to Rome. He is venerated as a saint.
did: Built the Leonine Wall around the Vatican
Victory over the Saracens at Ostia (849)

name: Benedict III
sum: Held firm against the imperially backed antipope Anastasius.
bio: Benedict was elected, then pushed aside by imperial envoys who installed Anastasius the Librarian. The Roman clergy and people refused to accept the intruder, and Benedict was consecrated. He received Æthelwulf of Wessex and his son Alfred in Rome.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Nicholas I
sum: “Nicholas the Great”: defended marriage and Church law against kings and bishops.
bio: Nicholas held that the pope’s authority extended over the whole Church. He refused to accept King Lothair II’s divorce, overruled powerful archbishops such as Hincmar of Reims and John of Ravenna, and protected the right of bishops to appeal to Rome. He refused to recognize Photius as Patriarch of Constantinople in place of the deposed Ignatius, beginning the Photian Schism. His answers to the newly baptized Bulgarians (866) are a model of pastoral wisdom: they reject torture and forced conversions and explain Christian customs gently.
did: Upheld the indissolubility of marriage against King Lothair II
Responses to the Bulgarians (866)
Opposed the uncanonical elevation of Photius
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Adrian II
sum: Approved the Slavonic liturgy of Sts. Cyril and Methodius.
bio: Adrian, elderly and once married, received Sts. Cyril and Methodius in Rome in 867-868, approved their Slavonic liturgical books and ordained Methodius a bishop for the Slavs. His legates presided at the Fourth Council of Constantinople (869-870), which deposed Photius. His wife and daughter were murdered by a relative of the antipope Anastasius.
did: Approved the Slavonic liturgy of Cyril and Methodius
Fourth Council of Constantinople (869-870)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John VIII
sum: Vigorous defender of Rome against the Saracens; the first pope said to have been murdered.
bio: John organized a papal fleet against Saracen raiders, crowned two emperors (Charles the Bald and Charles the Fat), defended St. Methodius when German bishops imprisoned him, and recognized Photius as patriarch after Ignatius’ death. According to the Annals of Fulda he was poisoned and then beaten to death by members of his own entourage, the first pope recorded as murdered.
did: Defended St. Methodius and the Slavonic liturgy
Organized defenses against Saracen raiders
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Marinus I
sum: The first bishop of another see to become pope.
bio: Marinus was the first man already bishop of another diocese (Caere) to be elected pope, then against church custom. He had been a legate at the council of 869-870. He restored Formosus to his see of Porto and favored the English school in Rome at King Alfred’s request.

name: Adrian III
sum: Died on his way to the Diet of Worms; venerated as a saint at Nonantola.
bio: Adrian’s short reign was marked by harsh punishment of his enemies in Rome. During a famine he cared for the poor. He died near Modena on his way to see Emperor Charles the Fat and was buried at the Abbey of Nonantola, where miracles were reported. His cult was confirmed in 1891.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen V
sum: Fed Rome in famine; forbade the Slavonic liturgy after Methodius’ death.
bio: Stephen found the papal treasury empty and fed the people from his family wealth during famine and locusts. He crowned Guy of Spoleto emperor (891). Misinformed by Methodius’ opponents, he forbade the Slavonic liturgy, and Methodius’ disciples were driven out of Moravia, taking their work to Bulgaria. He is also numbered Stephen VI.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Formosus
sum: Gifted missionary bishop whose corpse was put on trial in the “Cadaver Synod.”
bio: Formosus had been a missionary bishop to the Bulgarians and a papal diplomat before he fell out with John VIII. As pope he crowned Arnulf of Carinthia emperor against the Spoleto family. In 897 Stephen VI, under Spoleto pressure, had his corpse dug up, dressed in papal robes, put on trial and condemned, and thrown into the Tiber. The body was recovered and later reburied in St. Peter’s, and his ordinations were declared valid.
did: Missionary bishop to Bulgaria
Victim of the posthumous “Cadaver Synod” (897)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Boniface VI
sum: Elected by a Roman mob; reigned about fifteen days.
bio: Boniface had twice been degraded from holy orders for misconduct and was elected by rioting Romans after Formosus died. He died about two weeks later, possibly of gout. A council of 898 declared his election invalid, though he remains on the official list.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen VI
sum: Held the Cadaver Synod against Formosus; was then imprisoned and strangled.
bio: Stephen, made a bishop by Formosus, presided over the grotesque trial of his predecessor’s corpse in January 897. Shortly after, perhaps because the Lateran basilica collapsed, which was seen as a sign, the people rose against him. He was imprisoned and strangled. He is also numbered Stephen VII.
did: Presided over the Cadaver Synod (897)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Romanus
sum: Reigned about three months; probably deposed by the pro-Formosus party.
bio: Romanus seems to have reversed Stephen VI’s acts against Formosus. After about three months he was deposed and perhaps became a monk. Almost nothing else is known.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Theodore II
sum: Reburied Formosus with honor in St. Peter’s during a reign of twenty days.
bio: In his short reign Theodore held a synod that declared the Cadaver Synod invalid, restored clergy ordained by Formosus and reburied Formosus’ body, recovered from the Tiber, in St. Peter’s.
did: Reburied Formosus in St. Peter’s

name: John IX
sum: Banned trials of the dead and restored Formosus’ memory.
bio: A Benedictine monk, John held synods in Rome and Ravenna that confirmed the rehabilitation of Formosus, burned the records of the Cadaver Synod, forbade trying the dead and required that papal consecration take place in the presence of imperial envoys to prevent riots.
did: Forbade trials of the dead; burned the acts of the Cadaver Synod

name: Benedict IV
sum: Crowned Louis the Blind emperor; praised for his charity.
bio: Benedict, a supporter of Formosus, crowned Louis of Provence (“the Blind”) emperor in 901. The chronicler Flodoard praised his generosity to the poor. Little else is known of his reign.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo V
sum: Overthrown after about two months by the antipope Christopher.
bio: Leo, a parish priest from outside Rome, reigned briefly before he was imprisoned by his chaplain Christopher, who made himself antipope. Both were probably killed in prison in 904 on the orders of Sergius III.

name: Sergius III
sum: Seized the papacy with armed help and opened the era of the Theophylact family’s control.
bio: Sergius had been elected against Formosus’ party in 898 and driven out. In 904 he took Rome with armed support, revived the condemnation of Formosus and invalidated his ordinations, causing great confusion. His reign marks the start of decades of domination of Rome by the family of Theophylact and his wife Theodora, which hostile chroniclers called the “pornocracy.” He rebuilt the Lateran Basilica after its collapse.
did: Rebuilt the Lateran Basilica

name: Anastasius III
sum: Reigned under the control of Theophylact’s family.
bio: Little is known of Anastasius, who reigned for about two years while the Theophylact family controlled Rome. He granted the pallium to the bishop of Pavia and gave privileges to churches in Germany.

name: Lando
sum: The last pope with a name no earlier pope had used, until Francis in 2013.
bio: Lando is remembered mostly for his name: he was the last pope to bear a name not used by any earlier pope until Francis in 2013 (John Paul I in 1978 combined two existing names). Almost nothing is known of his reign of about seven months.

name: John X
sum: Led the Christian league that defeated the Saracens at the Garigliano; died in prison.
bio: John, Archbishop of Ravenna, was brought to Rome by the Theophylact family. He formed a league of Italian princes and Byzantines and personally took the field when it destroyed the Saracen base on the Garigliano river in 915. He crowned Berengar emperor and approved the Abbey of Cluny’s reforms. He later opposed Marozia, Theophylact’s daughter, who had him deposed, imprisoned and probably smothered in Castel Sant’Angelo.
did: Victory over the Saracens at the Garigliano (915)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo VI
sum: Installed by Marozia while John X was still in prison.
bio: Leo reigned about seven months under Marozia’s control. He confirmed the authority of the Archbishop of Spalato (Split) over Dalmatia, but little else is known.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Stephen VII
sum: Another pope of Marozia’s choosing.
bio: Stephen reigned about two years under Marozia’s influence and gave privileges to monasteries in France and Italy. He is also numbered Stephen VIII.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XI
sum: Son of Marozia, made pope in his early twenties, later held captive by his brother.
bio: John was Marozia’s son, by later tradition fathered by Pope Sergius III. In 932 his half-brother Alberic II overthrew Marozia and kept John under guard; he could act only in spiritual matters. He granted privileges to the Abbey of Cluny, helping the reform movement.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo VII
sum: A Benedictine monk who promoted Cluny’s reform with St. Odo.
bio: Chosen by Alberic II, Leo was a monk who invited St. Odo of Cluny to Rome to reform its monasteries. He named the Archbishop of Mainz papal vicar in Germany and advised against forced baptism of Jews.
did: Brought St. Odo of Cluny to reform Roman monasteries

name: Stephen VIII
sum: Supported the Carolingian king of France against rebel nobles.
bio: Stephen, elected under Alberic II, supported King Louis IV of France against his barons and continued support for monastic reform. A later story that he was mutilated by Alberic’s men is uncertain. He is also numbered Stephen IX.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Marinus II
sum: Reformed clergy and monasteries under Alberic’s protection.
bio: Marinus, a Roman priest chosen by Alberic II, worked to restore discipline among the clergy and helped monasteries recover. He is sometimes wrongly called Martin III.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Agapetus II
sum: Promoted church reform and missions north of the Alps.
bio: Agapetus, also chosen by Alberic, supported monastic reform and the missions in Scandinavia and among the Slavs, and settled disputes over the see of Reims. He declined Otto I’s request to come to Rome for crowning, at Alberic’s wish.

name: John XII
sum: Made pope at about eighteen; crowned Otto I and was later deposed by him.
bio: Octavian, son of Alberic II, became ruler of Rome and then pope as a teenager. Threatened by King Berengar, he called on Otto I and crowned him emperor in 962, re-founding the Western empire. Otto’s Privilegium confirmed the Papal States but required imperial consent for papal elections. John soon plotted against Otto, who had a synod depose him in 963 for scandalous conduct. John returned and took revenge on his enemies, and died in 964, according to the chronicler Liutprand in the act of adultery.
did: Crowned Otto I emperor (962)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Leo VIII
sum: A layman installed by Otto I after the deposition of John XII.
bio: Leo, a lay official, received all the holy orders in a single day and was installed by Otto I’s synod in 963 while John XII was still alive. His position was contested, and when the Romans elected Benedict V after John’s death, Otto restored Leo by force. Whether Leo or Benedict was the true pope is still unclear; the official list counts both.

name: Benedict V
sum: “The Grammarian,” chosen by the Romans and deposed by Otto I.
bio: Benedict, a learned deacon called “Grammaticus,” was elected by the Romans after John XII died. Otto I besieged Rome, deposed him and restored Leo VIII. Benedict was taken to Hamburg, where he lived with dignity under Archbishop Adaldag and died in 965 or 966. Otto III later brought his remains back to Rome.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XIII
sum: Crowned Otto II and created the Archdiocese of Magdeburg for the mission to the Slavs.
bio: John, Otto’s candidate, was driven out by Roman nobles and restored by the Emperor. He crowned Otto II co-emperor in 967 and married him to the Byzantine princess Theophanu in 972. He created the Archdiocese of Magdeburg (968) as a base for the mission to the Slavs and approved the bishopric of Prague.
did: Created the Archdiocese of Magdeburg (968)
Crowned Otto II and married him to Theophanu

name: Benedict VI
sum: Strangled in Castel Sant’Angelo on the orders of the noble Crescentius.
bio: After Otto I died, the Roman noble Crescentius and the deacon Franco (antipope Boniface VII) rose against Benedict. He was imprisoned in Castel Sant’Angelo and strangled in 974.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict VII
sum: Brought stability, fought simony and supported monastic reform.
bio: Benedict, a nephew of Alberic II, was installed with imperial support after the antipope Boniface VII fled. He held a synod against simony (981), supported Cluny and other reform monasteries, and promoted missions in Germany and the North.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XIV
sum: Chancellor of Otto II, starved or poisoned in prison by the antipope Boniface VII.
bio: Peter, Bishop of Pavia and chancellor of Otto II, took the name John to avoid the name of Peter. After the young emperor died in his arms, he lost protection; the antipope Boniface VII returned, imprisoned him in Castel Sant’Angelo, where he died, probably of starvation.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XV
sum: Carried out the first recorded papal canonization, of St. Ulrich of Augsburg.
bio: John, son of a priest, governed for over ten years under the control of the Roman noble Crescentius II. In 993 he solemnly declared Ulrich of Augsburg a saint, the first canonization by a pope that is documented. He mediated peace between England and Normandy (991).
did: First documented papal canonization: St. Ulrich (993)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory V
sum: The first German pope, cousin of Otto III, whom he crowned emperor.
bio: Bruno, cousin of Emperor Otto III, was appointed at about 24 and crowned Otto in 996. Crescentius II drove him from Rome and set up the antipope John XVI; Otto returned, and Crescentius was executed. Gregory imposed penance on King Robert II of France for an unlawful marriage.
did: First German pope
Crowned Otto III (996)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sylvester II
sum: Gerbert of Aurillac, the most learned man of his age and the first French pope.
bio: Gerbert studied mathematics in Catalonia, where he encountered Arabic learning; he taught at Reims, built an abacus and astronomical models, and helped spread Hindu-Arabic numerals in Latin Europe. He was tutor and friend of Otto III, who made him pope, and together they dreamed of a renewed Christian empire. He gave Hungary a crown and an archbishopric for St. Stephen and created the Archdiocese of Gniezno in Poland (1000). His learning made later legends call him a sorcerer.
did: First French pope; leading mathematician of his age
Founded the hierarchies of Poland (Gniezno, 1000) and Hungary (Esztergom)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XVII
sum: Reigned about six months under the control of John Crescentius.
bio: Elected under the domination of John Crescentius, he authorized a Polish mission to the Slavs. His number is a confusion: there was no John XVI as true pope (that was an antipope), but the count skipped ahead.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: John XVIII
sum: Created the Diocese of Bamberg; may have ended his life as a monk.
bio: John, a priest’s son, kept the peace with the Crescentii, approved the new Diocese of Bamberg founded by Emperor Henry II and briefly restored communion with Constantinople. He seems to have resigned and become a monk at St. Paul’s, where he died.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sergius IV
sum: Born Peter “Pig’s Snout”; cared for the poor in famine.
bio: Peter, nicknamed Bucca Porci, took the name Sergius. He supported the poor in a famine and gave privileges to monasteries. A bull calling for action after the Caliph destroyed the Church of the Holy Sepulchre (1009) is attributed to him, though its authenticity is disputed.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict VIII
sum: A layman of the Tusculum family who led armies and worked for reform with Henry II.
bio: A layman of the counts of Tusculum, Benedict defeated the rival Crescentii, crowned Henry II emperor in 1014 and allowed the Filioque to be sung in the Creed at Mass in Rome at Henry’s request. He fought the Saracens at Luni (1016) and backed Norman knights against the Byzantines in the south. With Henry he held the Synod of Pavia (1022) against clerical marriage and simony.
did: Crowned Henry II (1014); Filioque sung in the Roman Creed
Synod of Pavia on clerical reform (1022)
ic: Berasategui, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: John XIX
sum: Brother of Benedict VIII, made pope from layman in a day; crowned Conrad II.
bio: Romanus, brother of Benedict VIII, passed from layman to pope in a single day. He crowned Conrad II in 1027 in the presence of Kings Canute of England and Rudolph of Burgundy. He received the musician Guido of Arezzo, whose new way of writing music he admired, and he considered and abandoned a deal recognizing the Patriarch of Constantinople as “ecumenical.”
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict IX
sum: The only man to be pope three times (1032-1044, 1045, 1047-1048), and a scandal to the Church.
bio: Nephew of Benedict VIII and John XIX, Benedict was made pope in his early twenties by his family. His dissolute life led the Romans to drive him out in 1044 and elect Sylvester III; he returned in 1045, then sold the office to his godfather John Gratian (Gregory VI) and resigned. Emperor Henry III deposed all three claimants at Sutri (1046), but Benedict seized Rome again in 1047-1048 until he was driven out for good. He may have died a penitent at Grottaferrata. He is counted once in the official numbering, though his three terms appear separately in the list.
did: Reigned three separate times
His scandals helped spark the Gregorian Reform
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sylvester III
sum: Bishop of Sabina, set up against Benedict IX for about seven weeks.
bio: John, Bishop of Sabina, was elected when the Romans rose against Benedict IX. Benedict’s family drove him out within weeks, and he returned to his diocese. The Synod of Sutri (1046) deposed him. He is listed as pope, though some historians consider him an antipope.

name: Gregory VI
sum: Paid Benedict IX to resign, meaning well; deposed or resigned at Sutri.
bio: John Gratian, a respected archpriest, paid Benedict IX to resign in order to rid the Church of him, and was welcomed by reformers such as Peter Damian. At the Synod of Sutri (1046) Henry III treated the payment as simony, and Gregory resigned or was deposed. He went into exile in Germany with his chaplain Hildebrand, the future Gregory VII, whose choice of the name Gregory may honor him.
did: Synod of Sutri (1046)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Clement II
sum: Bishop of Bamberg, made pope by Henry III to begin reform; buried in Bamberg.
bio: Suidger, Bishop of Bamberg, was chosen by Henry III at Sutri and crowned him emperor on Christmas Day 1046. He held a synod against simony. He died after nine months, possibly of lead poisoning, and is the only pope buried in Germany, in Bamberg Cathedral.
did: Synod against simony (1047)
Only pope buried north of the Alps in Germany
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Damasus II
sum: Bishop of Brixen, died about three weeks after his consecration.
bio: Henry III’s second German pope, Poppo, Bishop of Brixen, had to wait for Benedict IX to be driven out. He died of malaria at Palestrina after only twenty-three days.

name: Leo IX
sum: The pope who launched the Gregorian Reform, traveling across Europe to hold councils.
bio: Bruno, Bishop of Toul, entered Rome as a barefoot pilgrim and accepted only after the Romans elected him. He gathered reformers around him, including Hildebrand, Humbert and Peter Damian, and turned the cardinals into an international body. He held synods in Italy, France and Germany against simony and clerical marriage. He led an army against the Normans and was captured at Civitate (1053). His legate Humbert excommunicated Patriarch Michael Cerularius in July 1054, three months after Leo’s death, an event traditionally taken as the start of the East-West Schism.
did: Launched the eleventh-century reform; traveling councils against simony
Legates’ excommunication of Cerularius (1054), the traditional start of the Great Schism

name: Victor II
sum: Henry III’s adviser and last imperial-appointed reform pope; regent for young Henry IV.
bio: Gebhard, Bishop of Eichstätt, continued Leo IX’s reforms. He was with Henry III when the Emperor died in 1056 and helped secure the succession of the child Henry IV. He died in Tuscany.

name: Stephen IX
sum: Abbot of Monte Cassino and determined reformer; made Peter Damian a cardinal.
bio: Frederick, brother of the Duke of Lorraine and a former legate in Constantinople in 1054, was abbot of Monte Cassino when elected. He pressed reform hard, named St. Peter Damian a cardinal, and died in Florence after eight months. He is also numbered Stephen X.

name: Nicholas II
sum: His decree of 1059 put papal elections in the hands of the cardinals.
bio: Gerard, Bishop of Florence, was elected by the reformers against the antipope Benedict X. His decree In Nomine Domini (1059) gave the cardinal bishops the leading role in electing the pope, removing it from Roman nobles and limiting the emperor’s part. He made the Normans papal vassals in southern Italy (Treaty of Melfi, 1059), and condemned Berengar of Tours’ teaching on the Eucharist.
did: Decree In Nomine Domini (1059): popes elected by the cardinals
Alliance with the Normans (Melfi, 1059)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Alexander II
sum: Reformer from Milan, elected by the cardinals; gave his banner to William of Normandy.
bio: Anselm had supported the Pataria reform movement in Milan. He was the first pope elected by the cardinals under the new decree, and he overcame the imperial antipope Honorius II.
