He supported reform across Europe, protected Jews in Spain from crusading violence, and sent a papal banner to William of Normandy for his invasion of England (1066).
did: First pope chosen under the 1059 election decree
Protected the Jews of Spain (1063)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory VII
sum: Hildebrand, the great reformer, who fought lay investiture and humbled Henry IV at Canossa.
bio: Hildebrand had served five popes before the Roman crowd acclaimed him pope. He fought simony and clerical marriage and banned lay investiture, the practice by which kings appointed bishops and gave them their ring and staff. Emperor Henry IV declared him deposed; Gregory excommunicated Henry, who came in penance to the castle of Canossa in January 1077 and stood in the snow until absolved. The conflict resumed, Henry took Rome in 1084, and Gregory, rescued by the Normans whose looting turned Romans against him, died in exile at Salerno, saying, “I have loved justice and hated iniquity, therefore I die in exile.” His Dictatus Papae sets out papal claims in 27 short sentences.
did: Banned lay investiture; struggle with Henry IV
Canossa (1077)
Gave his name to the Gregorian Reform
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Victor III
sum: Desiderius, the great abbot of Monte Cassino, who accepted the papacy unwillingly.
bio: Desiderius made Monte Cassino a center of art and learning, rebuilding its church with Byzantine craftsmen and collecting manuscripts that preserved classical texts. Elected after Gregory VII, he refused for a year and reigned only briefly. He supported an Italian expedition against the North African pirates at Mahdia (1087). He was beatified in 1887.
did: Abbot who made Monte Cassino a center of learning and art

name: Urban II
sum: Called the First Crusade at Clermont in 1095 and organized the papal Curia.
bio: Odo, a monk and prior of Cluny, continued Gregory VII’s reforms with more diplomacy. At the Council of Clermont (1095) he answered the Byzantine emperor’s appeal for help and called on Western knights to free the Christians of the East and Jerusalem, granting an indulgence to those who went with right intention. The First Crusade took Jerusalem in July 1099, two weeks before his death; the news did not reach him. He organized the papal government into the Roman Curia. He was beatified in 1881.
did: Proclaimed the First Crusade at Clermont (1095)
Organized the Roman Curia
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Paschal II
sum: Approved the Knights Hospitaller; captured by Henry V in the investiture struggle.
bio: Raniero, a monk, continued the investiture struggle. In 1111 Emperor Henry V seized him and forced him to grant the right of investiture, a concession a later synod revoked. He settled the conflict in England and France by compromise, and in 1113 recognized the Order of St. John (the Knights Hospitaller).
did: Recognized the Knights Hospitaller (1113)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gelasius II
sum: Attacked at his election by the Frangipani; died in exile at Cluny.
bio: John of Gaeta, long papal chancellor, was attacked and beaten by the Frangipani family during his election. Henry V set up an antipope and Gelasius fled to France, where he died at Cluny a year later.

name: Callixtus II
sum: Ended the investiture struggle with the Concordat of Worms and held the First Lateran Council.
bio: Guy, Archbishop of Vienne and a relative of kings, ended the Investiture Controversy with the Concordat of Worms (1122): the emperor gave up investing bishops with ring and staff, while being present at elections and investing them with their lands. The First Lateran Council (1123), the first ecumenical council held in the West, confirmed the settlement. He also issued Sicut Judaeis, protecting Jews from forced baptism and violence.
did: Concordat of Worms (1122)
First Lateran Council (1123)
Sicut Judaeis, protecting the Jews

name: Honorius II
sum: Approved the Premonstratensians and, through the Council of Troyes, the Knights Templar.
bio: Lambert, the cardinal who negotiated Worms, was installed amid a fight between the Frangipani and the Pierleoni families. He approved the Premonstratensian canons of St. Norbert (1126), and the Council of Troyes (1129), under his legate, approved the rule of the Knights Templar drawn up with St. Bernard.
did: Approved St. Norbert’s Premonstratensians (1126)
Knights Templar recognized at Troyes (1129)

name: Innocent II
sum: Overcame the schism of Anacletus II with St. Bernard’s help; held the Second Lateran Council.
bio: A minority of cardinals elected Gregory hastily, and the majority chose Anacletus II, who held Rome for eight years. St. Bernard of Clairvaux won Europe’s kings to Innocent’s side. After Anacletus died, the Second Lateran Council (1139) ended the schism and condemned simony and clerical marriage. He rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere, where he is buried, and condemned Peter Abelard (1140).
did: Second Lateran Council (1139)
Rebuilt Santa Maria in Trastevere
ic: Hugo DK, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Celestine II
sum: A learned pupil of Abelard who lifted the interdict on France.
bio: Guido, said to have studied under Abelard, lifted the interdict that Innocent II had placed on France. He reigned only about six months.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Lucius II
sum: Died of wounds received while leading an attack on the rebel Roman Senate.
bio: Lucius faced the Commune of Rome, which had set up a senate and rejected papal rule. He led an armed attack on the Capitol and, according to a later chronicle, was struck by stones and died of his injuries.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Eugene III
sum: The first Cistercian pope, a disciple of St. Bernard; launched the Second Crusade.
bio: Bernard of Pisa, a Cistercian monk and abbot of Tre Fontane, was a surprise choice. St. Bernard wrote him On Consideration, advice for a pope. He spent much of his reign away from the rebellious city of Rome, launched the Second Crusade (1145) after the fall of Edessa, and recognized the writings of St. Hildegard of Bingen. He was beatified in 1872.
did: First Cistercian pope
Called the Second Crusade (1145)
Encouraged St. Hildegard of Bingen
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Anastasius IV
sum: An elderly Roman who made peace in the city.
bio: Conrad, already about eighty, was a peacemaker. He settled disputes with Frederick Barbarossa over the see of Magdeburg and with England over the see of York, and gave privileges to the Knights Hospitaller.

name: Adrian IV
sum: The only English pope.
bio: Nicholas Breakspear left England poor, became abbot of St. Rufus near Avignon, and as legate reorganized the Church in Scandinavia. As pope he placed Rome under interdict to expel Arnold of Brescia, crowned Frederick Barbarossa (1155) and then clashed with him over whether the empire was a papal “benefice.” The bull Laudabiliter, said to grant Ireland to Henry II, is attributed to him, though its authenticity is debated.
did: The only English pope
Crowned Frederick Barbarossa (1155)

name: Alexander III
sum: Canon lawyer who outlasted Barbarossa’s antipopes and held the Third Lateran Council.
bio: Roland, a canon lawyer from Bologna, faced eighteen years of schism with antipopes supported by Frederick Barbarossa. Allied with the Lombard League, whose victory at Legnano (1176) defeated the Emperor, he made peace with Frederick at Venice in 1177. He imposed penance on Henry II for the murder of St. Thomas Becket and canonized Becket (1173). The Third Lateran Council (1179) required a two-thirds majority of cardinals to elect a pope, a rule still in force. He reserved canonizations to the Holy See.
did: Third Lateran Council (1179): two-thirds rule for papal elections
Canonized St. Thomas Becket (1173)
Peace of Venice with Barbarossa (1177)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Lucius III
sum: Issued Ad abolendam against heresy, a step toward the medieval Inquisition.
bio: Ubald, an elderly Cistercian, spent most of his reign outside Rome. With Barbarossa at Verona in 1184 he issued the decree Ad abolendam, which required bishops to seek out heretics such as the Cathars and Waldensians and hand the obstinate to secular rulers.
did: Decree Ad abolendam (1184)

name: Urban III
sum: Clashed with Barbarossa and died, by tradition, on hearing of the defeat at Hattin.
bio: Archbishop of Milan, Hubert was elected at Verona and never entered Rome. He quarreled with the Emperor over church property and the see of Trier. Tradition says he died of grief after the news of the Christian defeat at Hattin (July 1187), though Jerusalem itself fell just after his death.

name: Gregory VIII
sum: Called the Third Crusade with the bull Audita tremendi during a two-month reign.
bio: Albert, a canonist and chancellor, issued Audita tremendi soon after the fall of Jerusalem, calling Christians to repentance and to the Third Crusade. He made peace with Barbarossa and died at Pisa after fifty-seven days.
did: Bull Audita tremendi calling the Third Crusade (1187)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Clement III
sum: Made peace with the Roman Commune and returned the papacy to Rome.
bio: Paul, a Roman, ended the long quarrel with the Commune of Rome by a treaty in 1188, allowing the popes to live in the city again. He organized support for the Third Crusade and recognized the Scottish Church as directly subject to Rome.

name: Celestine III
sum: Ordained priest the day before his consecration, at about 85; crowned Henry VI.
bio: Hyacinth, a cardinal deacon for over forty years and once a defender of Abelard, was ordained priest only after his election, at about 85. He crowned Henry VI, approved the Teutonic Knights (1196) and excommunicated Duke Leopold of Austria for imprisoning King Richard the Lionheart.
did: Approved the Teutonic Order (1196)

name: Innocent III
sum: The most powerful medieval pope; approved St. Francis and held the Fourth Lateran Council.
bio: Lothar was elected at 37 and governed with energy across Christendom. He placed England under interdict until King John accepted Stephen Langton as Archbishop of Canterbury, and he arbitrated disputes among kings. He approved the first rule of St. Francis of Assisi (1209 or 1210) and encouraged St. Dominic. The Fourth Crusade he called turned against Constantinople (1204), which he condemned. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) defined transubstantiation, required yearly confession and Easter Communion, and reformed clergy. He also launched the Albigensian Crusade against the Cathars.
did: Fourth Lateran Council (1215): yearly confession, Easter Communion, transubstantiation
Approved St. Francis’ way of life (1209/1210)
Called the Fourth Crusade and the Albigensian Crusade
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Honorius III
sum: Approved the Dominicans (1216), the Franciscan Rule (1223) and the Carmelite rule.
bio: Cencio, a gentle and learned administrator, compiled papal decrees and the Liber censuum, a record of Church revenues. He confirmed the Order of Preachers of St. Dominic in 1216 and the Rule of St. Francis in 1223 (the Regula bullata, still in use), and approved the rule of the Carmelites (1226). He crowned Frederick II emperor and urged the Fifth Crusade.
did: Approved the Dominican Order (1216)
Approved the Franciscan Rule (1223)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory IX
sum: Friend of St. Francis; canonized him, issued the Decretals and created the papal Inquisition.
bio: Hugolino, nephew of Innocent III, was protector of the Franciscans and a friend of St. Francis and St. Clare. He canonized Francis (1228), Anthony of Padua (1232), Dominic (1234) and Elizabeth of Hungary (1235). He commissioned St. Raymond of Penyafort to compile the Decretals (1234), the core of Church law until 1917. He entrusted the hunt for heresy to Dominican and Franciscan inquisitors (1231), and fought long with Emperor Frederick II, whom he excommunicated twice.
did: Canonized Sts. Francis, Anthony, Dominic and Elizabeth
Decretals of Gregory IX (1234), basis of canon law until 1917
Papal Inquisition (1231)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Celestine IV
sum: Elected in the first “conclave,” locked in by a Roman senator; died seventeen days later.
bio: With Frederick II holding two cardinals prisoner, the ten remaining cardinals were locked in a ruinous palace in Rome by the senator Matteo Orsini, in heat and filth, until they chose an elderly Milanese, Godfrey. He died after seventeen days, before his coronation. The papacy then stood vacant for over eighteen months.

name: Innocent IV
sum: Great canon lawyer; deposed Frederick II at the First Council of Lyon.
bio: Sinibaldo, among the leading jurists of his age, fled to Lyon, where the First Council of Lyon (1245) declared Frederick II deposed. He sent Franciscan envoys, including John of Plano Carpini, to the Mongol Great Khan, gave cardinals their red hat, and sadly in 1252 authorized the use of torture by inquisitors in the bull Ad extirpanda.
did: First Council of Lyon (1245)
Sent envoys to the Mongols

name: Alexander IV
sum: Canonized St. Clare and defended the mendicant friars at Paris.
bio: Rinaldo, nephew of Gregory IX, canonized St. Clare of Assisi (1255), united several hermit groups into the Order of St. Augustine (the Grand Union, 1256), and defended the friars, including Sts. Thomas Aquinas and Bonaventure, against attacks at the University of Paris.
did: Canonized St. Clare (1255)
Grand Union of the Augustinian friars (1256)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Urban IV
sum: A shoemaker’s son who made Corpus Christi a feast for the whole Church.
bio: Jacques, son of a cobbler from Troyes, had been Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem. Moved by the visions of St. Juliana of Liège and the reports of the miracle of Bolsena, he extended the feast of Corpus Christi to the whole Church with the bull Transiturus (1264); St. Thomas Aquinas composed its texts. He invited Charles of Anjou to take the Kingdom of Sicily from the Hohenstaufen.
did: Instituted the feast of Corpus Christi (1264)

name: Clement IV
sum: A widower and former lawyer to the King of France; patron of Roger Bacon.
bio: Guy, a married lawyer in the service of St. Louis IX, became a priest after his wife died and rose to cardinal. As pope he crowned Charles of Anjou King of Sicily and asked the Franciscan Roger Bacon to send him his scientific works, the Opus Maius. His death began the longest vacancy in papal history, almost three years.
did: Patron of Roger Bacon’s Opus Maius

name: Gregory X
sum: Elected after nearly three years; created the conclave rules at the Second Council of Lyon.
bio: The vacancy lasted until the people of Viterbo locked in the cardinals, reduced their food and took off the roof of the palace. They chose Theobald, not a cardinal and then on crusade in Acre. At the Second Council of Lyon (1274), attended by St. Bonaventure (St. Thomas Aquinas died on the way), he achieved a brief reunion with the Greeks and issued Ubi periculum, creating the conclave: cardinals locked in, with food reduced if they delayed. He was beatified in 1713.
did: Second Council of Lyon (1274): brief reunion with the Greeks
Created the conclave (Ubi periculum)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Innocent V
sum: The first Dominican pope, a theologian and colleague of St. Thomas.
bio: Peter, a Dominican master at Paris, wrote a commentary on Peter Lombard’s Sentences and worked with St. Thomas on the order’s plan of studies. He preached at the funeral of St. Bonaventure. As pope for five months he tried to make peace among Italian cities. He was beatified in 1898.
did: First Dominican pope

name: Adrian V
sum: Died before being ordained priest, after suspending the strict conclave rules.
bio: Ottobuono, nephew of Innocent IV, had been legate in England and helped make peace between Henry III and his barons. Elected as a deacon, he suspended Gregory X’s conclave rules and died five weeks later, before being ordained priest or crowned.

name: John XXI
sum: The only Portuguese pope, a physician and author of a famous logic textbook.
bio: Peter of Spain is usually identified with the author of the Summulae logicales, the standard logic textbook of the late Middle Ages, and of the Thesaurus pauperum, a medical handbook. As pope he ordered an inquiry at Paris that led to Bishop Tempier’s condemnation of 219 propositions (1277). He died when the ceiling of a room he had added to the palace at Viterbo collapsed. He took the number XXI because of earlier confusion in the count of the Johns; there was no John XX.
did: Only Portuguese pope
Author of the Summulae logicales
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Nicholas III
sum: First pope to live at the Vatican; Dante placed him among the simoniacs.
bio: John, of the powerful Orsini family, made the Vatican the main papal residence and enlarged it. He issued Exiit qui seminat (1279), defining Franciscan poverty. He enriched his relatives so openly that Dante placed him head down among the simoniacs in the Inferno.
did: Made the Vatican the main papal residence
Exiit qui seminat on Franciscan poverty (1279)
ic: Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Martin IV
sum: A French pope who backed Charles of Anjou and broke the union with the Greeks.
bio: Simon, a former chancellor of France, was elected under Charles of Anjou’s pressure. He excommunicated Emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos, which wrecked the union of Lyon, and supported Charles after the Sicilian Vespers (1282). He is called Martin IV because two popes named Marinus were mistakenly counted as Martins.

name: Honorius IV
sum: Elderly Roman, crippled by gout, who encouraged the study of oriental languages.
bio: James, a grand-nephew of Honorius III, was so crippled by gout that he said Mass seated. He supported the Franciscan and Dominican missions and planned schools of Arabic and other languages at Paris for missionaries.

name: Nicholas IV
sum: The first Franciscan pope; sent the first missionaries to China.
bio: Jerome had been Minister General of the Franciscans. He sent John of Montecorvino to China (1289), where he became the first Archbishop of Peking, adorned Santa Maria Maggiore and the Lateran with mosaics, and founded the University of Montpellier. Acre, the last crusader stronghold, fell in 1291.
did: First Franciscan pope
Sent John of Montecorvino to China (1289)
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Celestine V
bur: Basilica of Santa Maria di Collemaggio, L’Aquila
sum: The hermit pope who resigned after five months; a saint.
bio: After a vacancy of over two years, the cardinals chose Peter of Morrone, an 84-year-old hermit and founder of the Celestine monks, after he wrote warning them of God’s judgment. Out of his depth and manipulated by Charles II of Naples, he issued a decree confirming a pope’s right to resign and then did so on 13 December 1294. His successor kept him confined at Fumone, where he died in 1296. He was canonized in 1313. He also established the Perdono of L’Aquila, a plenary indulgence still celebrated.
did: Resigned the papacy (1294), after confirming a pope may do so
Founded the Celestine monks; established the Perdono of L’Aquila
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Boniface VIII
sum: Proclaimed the first Jubilee (1300) and issued Unam Sanctam; humiliated at Anagni.
bio: Benedict, a brilliant canon lawyer, proclaimed the first Holy Year in 1300, drawing huge crowds of pilgrims to Rome. He published the Liber Sextus of canon law and founded the University of Rome (La Sapienza, 1303). He clashed with King Philip IV of France over taxing the clergy, issuing the bull Unam Sanctam (1302), which asserts that submission to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation. Philip’s agents seized him at Anagni in September 1303; he was freed by the townspeople but died weeks later.
did: First Jubilee Year (1300)
Bull Unam Sanctam (1302)
Founded the University of Rome (1303)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict XI
sum: Dominican Master who stood by Boniface VIII at Anagni; a peacemaker.
bio: Nicholas, son of a notary and Master General of the Dominicans, was one of two cardinals who stayed with Boniface VIII at Anagni. As pope he lifted some of Boniface’s penalties on France while excommunicating those who had assaulted Boniface. He died after eight months, possibly poisoned. He was beatified in 1736.

name: Clement V
sum: The first Avignon pope; suppressed the Knights Templar at the Council of Vienne.
bio: Bertrand, Archbishop of Bordeaux, was crowned in Lyon and never went to Rome; from 1309 he lived at Avignon, beginning about seventy years of papal residence there. Under pressure from Philip IV he allowed the trial of the Knights Templar and suppressed the order at the Council of Vienne (1311-1312) without condemning it. He founded universities and appointed many relatives as cardinals.
did: Began the Avignon papacy (1309)
Council of Vienne (1311-1312); suppression of the Templars
ic: Sailko, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: John XXII
sum: Organized the papal administration at Avignon; clashed with the Franciscan Spirituals.
bio: Elected at 72 after a two-year vacancy, Jacques ruled for eighteen years with great energy. He centralized church finances and appointments, canonized St. Thomas Aquinas (1323), and condemned the Franciscan Spirituals’ teaching that Christ and the Apostles owned nothing. Late in life he preached that the souls of the just would not see God until the Last Judgment; he withdrew this opinion on his deathbed, and his successor defined the opposite.
did: Canonized St. Thomas Aquinas (1323)
Organized the Curia at Avignon
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Benedict XII
sum: A Cistercian reformer who defined the beatific vision and began the Palace of the Popes.
bio: A Cistercian theologian, Jacques had led a careful inquisition in the Pyrenees whose records survive. His constitution Benedictus Deus (1336) defined that the souls of the just see God face to face before the final resurrection. He reformed the religious orders and began building the Palace of the Popes in Avignon.
did: Constitution Benedictus Deus on the beatific vision (1336)
Began the Palace of the Popes in Avignon
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Clement VI
sum: A generous, splendid pope who protected the Jews during the Black Death.
bio: Peter, a Benedictine and brilliant preacher, bought Avignon from Queen Joanna of Naples in 1348 and lived in lavish style. When the Black Death struck, he stayed at his post, provided for burials and care of the sick, and issued bulls (1348) condemning those who blamed the Jews for the plague and forbidding violence against them. He set Jubilees every fifty years and taught the doctrine of the Church’s treasury of merits (Unigenitus, 1343).
did: Protected the Jews during the Black Death (1348)
Purchased Avignon for the papacy
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Innocent VI
sum: A reforming lawyer who sent Cardinal Albornoz to recover the Papal States.
bio: Stephen cut back the luxury of the Avignon court and sent Cardinal Gil Álvarez de Albornoz to Italy, who reconquered the Papal States and issued their constitutions (1357). He helped negotiate the Treaty of Brétigny between England and France (1360).
did: Recovered the Papal States through Cardinal Albornoz
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Urban V
sum: A Benedictine abbot who briefly brought the papacy back to Rome.
bio: William, abbot of Saint-Victor in Marseille, kept living as a monk. He returned to Rome in 1367, the first pope there in sixty years, and received the Byzantine emperor John V Palaiologos, who professed the Catholic faith. Unrest in Italy and the French cardinals drew him back to Avignon in 1370, against the warnings of St. Bridget of Sweden, and he died soon after. He founded universities and colleges. He was beatified in 1870.
did: Returned to Rome (1367-1370)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory XI
sum: Returned the papacy to Rome in 1377, urged by St. Catherine of Siena.
bio: Nephew of Clement VI, Peter was made a cardinal at about 18 and became a fine canonist. Urged by St. Catherine of Siena, who came to Avignon, he returned the papal court to Rome, entering on 17 January 1377. He condemned propositions of John Wycliffe (1377). He was the last French pope.
did: Returned the papacy to Rome (1377)
Last French pope
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Urban VI
sum: His harsh rule led French cardinals to elect a rival, starting the Great Western Schism.
bio: Bartholomew, a capable official, was elected while a Roman crowd demanded an Italian. His violent temper alienated the cardinals; within months most of them declared his election invalid and chose Clement VII, who went to Avignon. Europe split between the two obediences. Urban later had five cardinals suspected of conspiracy tortured and killed. The Church recognizes him as the lawful pope.
did: Beginning of the Western Schism (1378)
ic: Kostisl, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Boniface IX
sum: Roman pope of the Schism who held the Jubilees of 1390 and 1400.
bio: Peter, elected young, restored papal control over Rome and the Papal States, fortified Castel Sant’Angelo and celebrated Jubilees in 1390 and 1400. He raised money by selling offices and indulgences, which damaged his name. He refused proposals for both popes to resign.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Innocent VII
sum: Restored the University of Rome during the Schism.
bio: Cosimo, a learned lawyer, promised to work to end the Schism but did little. He reorganized the University of Rome, adding the study of Greek. Riots forced him to flee Rome for a time.

name: Gregory XII
sum: Resigned at the Council of Constance so the Western Schism could end.
bio: Angelo, about eighty, was elected on condition that he would resign if his rival did. The two never met, and in 1409 the Council of Pisa deposed both and elected a third, making three claimants. In 1415 Gregory formally convoked the Council of Constance and then resigned, opening the way to a single election. He was the last pope to resign until Benedict XVI in 2013.
did: Convoked and resigned before the Council of Constance (1415)
Last pope to resign until 2013

name: Martin V
sum: Elected at Constance, ending the Western Schism; rebuilt a ruined Rome.
bio: Oddo, of the Roman Colonna family, was elected on St. Martin’s Day 1417 by the cardinals and representatives of the nations at the Council of Constance, ending the Schism. He returned to a ruined Rome in 1420 and began restoring its churches, streets and government. He resisted the idea that councils stood above the pope and opposed the Hussites.
did: End of the Western Schism (1417)
Restored Rome after the Schism
ic: Sailko (photographer); Lorenzo di Bicci (artist), CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons, file page

name: Eugene IV
sum: Presided over the Council of Florence, which reunited the Greek and Latin Churches for a time.
bio: Gabriel, a Venetian nephew of Gregory XII, spent years in conflict with the Council of Basel, which claimed authority over the pope and finally elected an antipope. Eugene moved the council to Ferrara and then Florence (1438-1445), where the Byzantine emperor and Greek bishops agreed to reunion with Rome in Laetentur caeli (1439). Unions with the Armenians, Copts and others followed. The union with the Greeks did not last after the fall of Constantinople, but the council’s decrees on the sacraments and on papal primacy remained important.
did: Council of Florence: reunion with the Greeks (Laetentur caeli, 1439)
Decree for the Armenians on the seven sacraments (1439)

docs.s: vir Dei

name: Nicholas V
sum: The first Renaissance pope; founded the Vatican Library.
bio: Thomas, a scholar and book collector, ended the Basel schism when the antipope Felix V resigned (1449), and celebrated the Jubilee of 1450. He gathered Greek and Latin manuscripts, many saved from the East, and founded the Vatican Library. He planned the rebuilding of St. Peter’s and the Vatican. Constantinople fell to the Ottomans in 1453 during his reign.
did: Founded the Vatican Library
Ended the schism of Basel (1449)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Callixtus III
sum: The first Borgia pope; reopened Joan of Arc’s case, which declared her innocent.
bio: Alfonso, a Spanish canon lawyer, worked to raise a crusade against the Ottomans; the victory at Belgrade (1456) led him to order the noon bells and extend the feast of the Transfiguration. He authorized the retrial that declared Joan of Arc innocent (1456). He made his nephew Rodrigo, later Alexander VI, a cardinal.
did: Annulment of Joan of Arc’s condemnation (1456)
Feast of the Transfiguration extended to the whole Church (1457)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pius II
sum: Humanist writer who became pope, rebuilt his birthplace as Pienza, and died organizing a crusade.
bio: Aeneas Silvius was a famous humanist, poet and diplomat who had supported the Council of Basel before changing sides and becoming a priest. As pope he condemned appeals from the pope to a future council (Execrabilis, 1460). He rebuilt his native village as the model town of Pienza and wrote his Commentaries, the only autobiography by a pope in office. He died at Ancona waiting for a crusading fleet that never came.
did: Bull Execrabilis (1460)
Wrote his Commentaries; built Pienza

name: Paul II
sum: Built the Palazzo Venezia; quarreled with the humanists of the Roman Academy.
bio: Peter, nephew of Eugene IV, built the Palazzo San Marco (now Palazzo Venezia). He suppressed the Roman Academy of humanists on suspicion of paganism and plotting. He set the Jubilee interval at 25 years, introduced carnival races on the Via del Corso, and first had cardinals wear red caps.
did: Set Jubilees every 25 years
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Sixtus IV
sum: Franciscan theologian who built the Sistine Chapel and opened the Vatican Library to scholars.
bio: Francis, Minister General of the Franciscans and a respected theologian, built the Sistine Chapel, named after him, and Ponte Sisto; he opened the Vatican Library to scholars and founded the Capitoline Museums. He approved the feast of the Immaculate Conception. He also practiced lavish nepotism, was involved in the Pazzi conspiracy against the Medici (1478), and authorized the Spanish Inquisition (1478), whose abuses he later protested.
did: Built the Sistine Chapel
Founded the Capitoline Museums
Authorized the Spanish Inquisition (1478)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Innocent VIII
sum: Openly favored his children; his bull of 1484 encouraged the witch hunts.
bio: John Baptist, father of children born before his ordination, married his son into the Medici family. His bull Summis desiderantes (1484) gave authority to two inquisitors in Germany, one of whom wrote the notorious Malleus maleficarum. He kept the Ottoman prince Cem as a hostage in return for payments from the Sultan.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Alexander VI
sum: Rodrigo Borgia: able administrator, notorious for his mistresses and his children.
bio: Rodrigo, nephew of Callixtus III, served as vice-chancellor for 35 years. His election was secured with promises and gifts. He openly advanced his children, including Cesare and Lucrezia Borgia. He issued Inter caetera (1493) dividing new lands between Spain and Portugal, celebrated the Jubilee of 1500 and had Girolamo Savonarola, his fierce critic, excommunicated; Florence executed the friar in 1498.
did: Inter caetera on the new lands (1493)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Pius III
sum: Nephew of Pius II, a reformer who died 26 days after his election.
bio: Francis was respected for his upright life and learning, and built the Piccolomini Library in Siena Cathedral. Old and ill, he was ordained priest and bishop after his election and died within a month.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Julius II
bur: St. Peter’s Basilica (San Pietro in Vincoli has his monument)
sum: The “warrior pope” who began the new St. Peter’s and commissioned Michelangelo and Raphael.
bio: Julian, nephew of Sixtus IV, led armies in person to recover the Papal States and drive the French from Italy. He laid the foundation stone of the new St. Peter’s Basilica (1506) designed by Bramante, commissioned Michelangelo to paint the Sistine Chapel ceiling (1508-1512) and Raphael to fresco the Vatican rooms, and founded the Swiss Guard (1506). He called the Fifth Lateran Council (1512).
did: Laid the foundation of the new St. Peter’s (1506)
Commissioned the Sistine Chapel ceiling and the Raphael Rooms
Founded the Swiss Guard (1506)
ic: National Gallery of Denmark, public domain, Europeana

name: Leo X
sum: Son of Lorenzo the Magnificent; excommunicated Martin Luther.
bio: John, made a cardinal at 13, was a cultivated patron of art and learning. He closed the Fifth Lateran Council (1517), made the Concordat of Bologna with France (1516), and preached an indulgence to fund St. Peter’s, against which Luther posted his 95 Theses in 1517. He condemned Luther’s errors in Exsurge Domine (1520) and excommunicated him (1521). He gave Henry VIII the title “Defender of the Faith.”
did: Excommunicated Martin Luther (1521)
Concluded the Fifth Lateran Council (1517)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Adrian VI
sum: The last non-Italian pope until John Paul II; admitted the Church’s guilt in the crisis.
bio: Adrian, a theologian from Louvain and tutor of Emperor Charles V, kept his own name as pope. Austere and reforming, he instructed his legate at the Diet of Nuremberg (1522) to confess that the evils of the Church had begun “in the Roman Curia.” He died before his reforms could take hold, and was the last non-Italian pope until 1978.
did: Admitted the Curia’s guilt in the Church’s crisis (1522)
Last non-Italian pope until 1978
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Clement VII
sum: Pope during the Sack of Rome (1527) and Henry VIII’s break with Rome.
bio: Julius, cousin of Leo X, was caught between France and Charles V. In 1527 Imperial troops sacked Rome while he took refuge in Castel Sant’Angelo; the Swiss Guard died defending him. He refused to annul Henry VIII’s marriage to Catherine of Aragon, and England broke with Rome. He commissioned Michelangelo’s Last Judgment and approved the Capuchins (1528).
did: Sack of Rome (1527)
Refused Henry VIII’s annulment; English schism
Approved the Capuchin Franciscans (1528)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Paul III
sum: Opened the Council of Trent and approved the Jesuits.
bio: Alexander, a Renaissance prince with children born before his ordination, became the first pope of the Catholic Reform. He named reforming cardinals such as Contarini, Pole and Carafa, approved the Society of Jesus (1540), set up the Roman Inquisition (1542) and opened the Council of Trent (1545). In Sublimis Deus (1537) he declared that the peoples of the Americas are true human beings who must not be enslaved. He commissioned Michelangelo to complete St. Peter’s.
did: Opened the Council of Trent (1545)
Approved the Society of Jesus (1540)
Sublimis Deus on the dignity of the American peoples (1537)
ic: Catholic University of Leuven, public domain, Europeana

name: Julius III
sum: Reopened the Council of Trent; built the Villa Giulia.
bio: John Mary, a former president of Trent, reopened the council (1551-1552) and confirmed the Jesuits again. Mary Tudor restored Catholicism in England in his time. He built the Villa Giulia and named Palestrina choirmaster of the Julian Chapel. His favor to a young adopted relative was a scandal.
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Marcellus II
sum: Reformer who reigned 22 days; Palestrina’s Missa Papae Marcelli honors him.
bio: Marcellus, a learned reformer and former president of Trent, kept his own name and began cutting the court’s expenses. He died after three weeks. Palestrina’s famous Mass for Pope Marcellus was dedicated to his memory.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Paul IV
sum: Severe reformer; co-founder of the Theatines, he created the Roman ghetto and the Index.
bio: John Peter co-founded the Theatine order with St. Cajetan. As pope, at 79, he fought corruption fiercely but harshly. He confined the Jews of Rome to a ghetto (Cum nimis absurdum, 1555), issued the first Roman Index of Forbidden Books (1559), and fought a disastrous war with Spain. The Romans rioted at his death.
did: Co-founded the Theatines
First Roman Index of Forbidden Books (1559)
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Pius IV
sum: Closed the Council of Trent with the help of his nephew St. Charles Borromeo.
bio: John Angelo (not of the Florentine Medici) reconvened the Council of Trent in 1562, guided by his nephew St. Charles Borromeo, and closed it in 1563. He confirmed its decrees, issued the Profession of Faith of Trent (1564) and a new Index. He commissioned Michelangelo to turn the Baths of Diocletian into Santa Maria degli Angeli.
did: Concluded and confirmed the Council of Trent (1563-1564)
Tridentine Profession of Faith (1564)
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Pius V
sum: Dominican saint who carried out Trent: the Catechism, Breviary and Missal; the victory of Lepanto.
bio: Michael Ghislieri, a shepherd boy who became a Dominican friar and Grand Inquisitor, lived as a friar while pope. He put the Council of Trent into effect: the Roman Catechism (1566), the Breviary (1568) and the Roman Missal (Quo primum, 1570), which remained in use until 1970. He named St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church. He formed the Holy League that defeated the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto (7 October 1571), asked Christians to pray the Rosary for victory, and established the feast of Our Lady of Victory, now Our Lady of the Rosary. He excommunicated Elizabeth I of England (1570). Canonized in 1712.
did: Roman Catechism (1566), Breviary (1568) and Missal (1570)
Holy League and the victory of Lepanto (1571); feast of the Rosary
Declared St. Thomas Aquinas a Doctor of the Church (1567)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory XIII
sum: Gave the world the Gregorian calendar (1582) and founded the Gregorian University.
bio: Hugh, a law professor and former member of the Council of Trent, became a reformer after ordination. He introduced the Gregorian calendar in 1582, dropping ten days to bring Easter back in line with the seasons. He founded the Roman College (now the Gregorian University) and many national colleges for training priests, including the German and English Colleges, and expanded the network of nuncios. He also ordered a Te Deum after the St. Bartholomew’s Day Massacre (1572), a lasting stain on his memory.
did: Gregorian calendar (1582)
Founded the Gregorian University and the national colleges in Rome
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Sixtus V
sum: Franciscan swineherd’s son who rebuilt Rome and organized the Curia into congregations.
bio: Felix, born poor, became a Franciscan preacher. In five years he cleared the Papal States of bandits, laid out the straight streets that join Rome’s great basilicas, raised the Egyptian obelisks, including the one in St. Peter’s Square, completed the dome of St. Peter’s and built the Acqua Felice aqueduct. He fixed the College of Cardinals at seventy and organized the Curia into fifteen congregations (1588).
did: Reorganized the Curia into congregations (1588)
Completed the dome of St. Peter’s; raised the Vatican obelisk
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Urban VII
sum: The shortest reign in papal history: thirteen days.
bio: John Baptist, a respected diplomat, died of malaria before his coronation. In his few days he banned tobacco use in and near churches, the first known smoking ban, and left his fortune to provide dowries for poor girls.
did: Shortest pontificate in history (13 days)
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Gregory XIV
sum: Supported the Catholic League in France against the Protestant Henry of Navarre.
bio: Nicholas, a friend of St. Charles Borromeo and St. Philip Neri, sent money and troops to the Catholic League in France and renewed the excommunication of Henry of Navarre. He ordered that cardinals be given the red biretta and forbade betting on papal elections.
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Innocent IX
sum: A reforming lawyer who reigned two months.
bio: John Anthony, a canonist who had attended Trent, reorganized the Secretariat of State into sections before dying two months after his election.
ic: Wikimedia Commons, public domain, file page

name: Clement VIII
sum: Reconciled Henry IV of France and published the Clementine Vulgate.
bio: Hippolytus, a friend and penitent of St. Philip Neri, absolved Henry IV of France after his conversion (1595), ending the French wars of religion. He issued the Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592), the official Latin Bible until 1979, and revised liturgical books. The Union of Brest (1595-1596) brought the Ruthenian Church into communion with Rome. Giordano Bruno was burned in Rome during his reign (1600).
did: Sixto-Clementine Vulgate (1592)
Union of Brest with the Ruthenian Church (1595)
ic: Rijksmuseum, public domain, Europeana

name: Leo XI
sum: A Medici reformer, disciple of St. Philip Neri, who died after 27 days.
bio: Alexander, a disciple of St. Philip Neri, caught a chill during the ceremony of taking possession of the Lateran and died less than a month after his election.

bio: Gregory Chiaramonti, a Benedictine, was elected in Venice in 1800 while Rome was occupied. He signed the Concordat of 1801 with Napoleon, restoring the Church in France, and attended Napoleon’s coronation (1804). When he refused to join the blockade against England, the French annexed the Papal States (1809) and held him prisoner at Savona and Fontainebleau for five years. He returned to Rome in 1814, restored the Society of Jesus (Sollicitudo omnium ecclesiarum) and, after Napoleon’s fall, sheltered members of Napoleon’s family. His cause of beatification is open.

bio: Maurus Cappellari, a Camaldolese monk and Prefect of Propaganda Fide, was the last pope not already a bishop when elected. He faced revolution in the Papal States and resisted liberal ideas, condemning the views of Lamennais in Mirari vos (1832). He gave a strong push to the missions, creating many dioceses and vicariates, and condemned the slave trade in In supremo apostolatus (1839). He founded the Etruscan and Egyptian museums in the Vatican. His opposition to railways, which he called “chemins d’enfer,” is often quoted.

sum: The longest documented reign; defined the Immaculate Conception and held the First Vatican Council.
bio: Pio Nono began as a reformer welcomed by liberals, but the revolution of 1848, the murder of his minister Pellegrino Rossi and his flight to Gaeta changed him. He defined the dogma of the Immaculate Conception (Ineffabilis Deus, 1854) and issued the Syllabus of Errors with Quanta cura (1864). He restored the Catholic hierarchy in England (1850) and the Netherlands (1853). The First Vatican Council (1869-1870) defined papal primacy and infallibility (Pastor Aeternus) and taught on faith and reason (Dei Filius). Italian troops took Rome on 20 September 1870, ending the Papal States, and Pius lived as a “prisoner in the Vatican.” His reign of 31 years and 7 months is the longest documented in history. He was beatified in 2000.

name: Leo XIII
sum: Founder of modern Catholic social teaching with Rerum Novarum; revived the study of St. Thomas.
bio: Elected at 67 and expected to be a short “caretaker,” Leo reigned 25 years and wrote 86 encyclicals. Aeterni Patris (1879) restored the philosophy of St. Thomas Aquinas to Catholic schools. Rerum Novarum (1891) defended the rights of workers to a just wage and to form unions, and the right of private property, against both unbridled capitalism and socialism, founding modern Catholic social teaching. He opened the Vatican Secret Archives to scholars (1881), encouraged biblical studies (Providentissimus Deus, 1893), promoted the Rosary in twelve encyclicals, wrote the Prayer to St. Michael, and consecrated the world to the Sacred Heart (1899). He declared Anglican orders invalid (Apostolicae curae, 1896). He was the first pope filmed and recorded.

name: Pius X
sum: The parish-priest pope: frequent Communion, children’s First Communion, and the fight against Modernism.
bio: Joseph Sarto, a postman’s son, was a parish priest, seminary director, Bishop of Mantua and Patriarch of Venice. His motto was “to restore all things in Christ.” He encouraged frequent, even daily, Communion (1905) and lowered the age of First Communion to the age of reason (Quam singulari, 1910). He reformed church music, restoring Gregorian chant (Tra le sollecitudini, 1903), reformed the Breviary, and began the codification of canon law. He condemned Modernism in Lamentabili and Pascendi (1907) and required the anti-modernist oath (1910). He opposed the French law separating Church and State (1905). He died at the start of the First World War, grieving over it. He was canonized in 1954, the first pope canonized since Pius V.

sum: The peace pope of the First World War; promulgated the 1917 Code of Canon Law.
bio: Giacomo della Chiesa, a diplomat and Archbishop of Bologna, was elected a month after the war began. He called it “the suicide of civilized Europe,” kept the Holy See neutral, and in August 1917 sent a peace note to the warring nations proposing disarmament, arbitration and the restoration of occupied lands; it was ignored. He set up an office that helped prisoners of war and their families and spent the Vatican’s funds on relief, leaving it nearly bankrupt. He promulgated the first Code of Canon Law (1917). Maximum illud (1919) called for native clergy in mission lands. A statue raised by grateful Turks in Istanbul honors him as “benefactor of the peoples.”

sum: Signed the Lateran Treaty creating Vatican City; condemned Nazism and Communism.
bio: Achille Ratti, a scholar, librarian of the Ambrosian and Vatican libraries, and mountaineer, had been nuncio in Poland. He instituted the feast of Christ the King (Quas primas, 1925), promoted Catholic Action, and wrote on Christian marriage (Casti connubii, 1930) and the social order (Quadragesimo anno, 1931). The Lateran Treaty with Italy (1929) settled the “Roman Question” and created the independent State of Vatican City. In 1937 he condemned Nazism in Mit brennender Sorge, smuggled into Germany and read from every pulpit, and atheistic Communism in Divini Redemptoris. He founded Vatican Radio with Marconi (1931). He said in 1938, “Spiritually, we are all Semites.”

name: Pius XII
sum: Led the Church through the Second World War and defined the Assumption of Mary.
bio: Eugenio Pacelli, a Roman diplomat, had been nuncio in Germany and Secretary of State. Elected on his 63rd birthday months before the war, he tried to prevent it and then worked for refugees and prisoners. His Christmas message of 1942 spoke of hundreds of thousands killed “because of their nationality or race.” Church institutions in Rome, including the Vatican and Castel Gandolfo, sheltered thousands of Jews during the German occupation. His public restraint during the Holocaust has been debated ever since; the Vatican archives for his reign were opened in 2020. His encyclicals renewed teaching on the Church as the Mystical Body (Mystici Corporis, 1943), opened Catholic biblical scholarship (Divino afflante Spiritu, 1943) and the liturgy (Mediator Dei, 1947). He defined the dogma of the Assumption (Munificentissimus Deus, 1950) and restored the Easter Vigil (1951-1955). He was declared Venerable in 2009.

name: John XXIII
sum: “Good Pope John,” who called the Second Vatican Council.
bio: Angelo Roncalli, the fourth of thirteen children of sharecroppers, served as a military chaplain in the First World War and spent twenty years as a papal diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece, where he helped save Jews during the Second World War, and then in France. Patriarch of Venice at 71, he was elected at nearly 77 as a supposed caretaker. Three months later he announced an ecumenical council, which opened on 11 October 1962. He wrote Mater et Magistra (1961) on social justice and Pacem in Terris (1963), addressed “to all men of good will,” on human rights and peace, after helping to calm the Cuban Missile Crisis. His warmth, visits to prisons and hospitals and “moonlight speech” made him beloved. He died of cancer between the Council’s first and second sessions. He was canonized in 2014.

name: Paul VI
bn: Giovanni Battista Enrico Antonio Maria Montini
sum: Guided the Second Vatican Council to its end and wrote Humanae Vitae; the first pope to travel by plane.
bio: Giovanni Battista Montini worked for thirty years in the Secretariat of State and was Archbishop of Milan. As pope he reopened and concluded the Second Vatican Council (1965), promulgating its sixteen documents, and then carried out its reforms, including the new Roman Missal (1969). He embraced Patriarch Athenagoras in Jerusalem (1964), and together they lifted the excommunications of 1054. He was the first pope to fly and visited six continents, speaking at the United Nations in 1965 (“No more war, war never again!”). He wrote Ecclesiam Suam (1964), Populorum Progressio (1967) on development, and Humanae Vitae (1968), reaffirming the Church’s teaching on contraception amid fierce opposition. Evangelii Nuntiandi (1975) remains a charter for evangelization. He created the Synod of Bishops and internationalized the Curia. He was canonized in 2018.

name: John Paul I
sum: “The smiling pope,” who reigned 33 days.
bio: Albino Luciani, son of a migrant worker who was a socialist, was a teacher of seminarians, Bishop of Vittorio Veneto and Patriarch of Venice, where he wrote Illustrissimi, witty letters to famous figures from Dickens to Pinocchio. He was the first pope to take a double name, honoring his two predecessors, and refused a coronation, beginning his ministry with a simple Mass. In his few general audiences he spoke of humility, faith, hope and charity with stories and humor. He died suddenly of a heart attack on the night of 28 September 1978. He was beatified in 2022.

name: John Paul II
sum: The first Polish pope: philosopher, pilgrim to 129 countries, and witness against Communism.
bio: Karol Wojtyła lost his mother, brother and father by the age of 20. Under Nazi occupation he worked in a quarry and chemical plant, acted in an underground theater and studied for the priesthood in secret. A philosopher and poet, he became Archbishop of Kraków. Elected at 58, the first non-Italian since 1523, he told the world “Be not afraid!” His first visit to Poland (1979) helped give rise to the Solidarity movement and the peaceful fall of Communism in 1989. He survived an assassination attempt in St. Peter’s Square on 13 May 1981 and forgave his attacker in his prison cell. He made 104 foreign journeys to 129 countries, began World Youth Day, and canonized 482 saints. His 14 encyclicals include Redemptor Hominis, Laborem Exercens, Veritatis Splendor, Evangelium Vitae and Fides et Ratio; his Wednesday talks became the Theology of the Body. He promulgated the 1983 Code of Canon Law and the Catechism of the Catholic Church (1992), prayed at the Western Wall and asked forgiveness for the sins of Christians in the Jubilee of 2000, and added the Luminous Mysteries to the Rosary (2002). He endured Parkinson’s disease in public and died on the vigil of Divine Mercy Sunday 2005, a feast he had established. Crowds cried “Santo subito!” He was canonized in 2014.

name: Benedict XVI
sum: Theologian pope who taught that “God is love,” and the first pope to resign in nearly 600 years.
bio: Joseph Ratzinger, son of a Bavarian policeman, was drafted into the German anti-aircraft auxiliary as a teenager and deserted at the end of the war. He became one of the leading theologians of his generation, an adviser at the Second Vatican Council, Archbishop of Munich, and for 24 years Prefect of the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under John Paul II, overseeing the Catechism. Elected at 78, he called himself “a simple, humble laborer in the vineyard of the Lord.” His encyclicals Deus Caritas Est (2005), Spe Salvi (2007) and Caritas in Veritate (2009) treated love, hope and charity in truth; his three-volume Jesus of Nazareth was written as a personal work. He freed wider use of the 1962 Missal (Summorum Pontificum, 2007), created ordinariates for former Anglicans (Anglicanorum Coetibus, 2009), beatified John Henry Newman, met victims of abuse and strengthened the Church’s procedures against it, and spoke on faith and reason at Regensburg (2006). On 11 February 2013 he announced his resignation, citing failing strength, and lived as Pope Emeritus in the Vatican until his death on 31 December 2022.

name: Francis
bur: Basilica of Santa Maria Maggiore, Rome
sum: The first pope from the Americas and the first Jesuit pope, who called the Church to mercy and to the peripheries.
bio: Jorge Mario Bergoglio, son of Italian immigrants, worked as a chemical technician before joining the Jesuits. He was Jesuit provincial of Argentina during the dictatorship and later Archbishop of Buenos Aires, known for riding the bus and visiting the slums. The first pope to take the name Francis, after St. Francis of Assisi, he lived in the Casa Santa Marta guesthouse rather than the papal apartment. Evangelii Gaudium (2013) set out his program of a missionary Church; Laudato si’ (2015) addressed care for our common home; Amoris Laetitia (2016) followed two synods on the family; Fratelli Tutti (2020) addressed fraternity and social friendship; Dilexit Nos (2024) the Sacred Heart. He proclaimed an extraordinary Jubilee of Mercy (2015-2016), reformed the Curia (Praedicate Evangelium, 2022) and Vatican finances, strengthened laws against abuse (Vos Estis Lux Mundi, 2019), signed the Document on Human Fraternity with the Grand Imam of al-Azhar (2019), and held a long Synod on synodality (2021-2024). He prayed alone in an empty St. Peter’s Square during the pandemic (27 March 2020). He opened the Jubilee of 2025, blessed the crowds on Easter Sunday, and died the next morning. At his request he was buried in Santa Maria Maggiore, the first pope buried outside the Vatican in over a century.

name: Leo XIV
sum: The first pope from the United States, an Augustinian missionary to Peru.
bio: Robert Prevost grew up in Dolton, near Chicago, studied mathematics at Villanova University and joined the Order of St. Augustine in 1977. After studying canon law in Rome he spent much of his life in Peru as a missionary, teacher, judicial vicar and seminary formator, then led the Augustinians worldwide as Prior General for twelve years (2001-2013). He returned to Peru as Bishop of Chiclayo and became a Peruvian citizen. Francis named him Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops in 2023. Elected on 8 May 2025 on the fourth ballot, he greeted the world with “Peace be with all of you” and chose the name Leo in honor of Leo XIII and his social teaching, in view of a new industrial revolution brought by artificial intelligence. His motto, In Illo uno unum (“In the One, we are one”), comes from St. Augustine. He brought the Jubilee of 2025 to its close, issued the apostolic exhortation Dilexi Te on love for the poor (2025) and an apostolic letter for the 1700th anniversary of the Council of Nicaea, which he marked with a visit to Turkey. His first encyclical, Magnifica Humanitas (2026), applies the Church’s social teaching to safeguarding the human person in the age of artificial intelligence.
